Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Such a framework is dubbed 'pdf4lhc', an open-source suite of code designed to streamline the incorporation of PDF estimates by enabling the automatic loading of PDF sets, application of evolution equations, and combination of contributions from various sources, ultimately producing a unified set of integrated predictions. This development aims to simplify the PDF fitting process and make it more accessible to a broader research community. The 'pdf4lhc' suite is initially demonstrated through successful applications in fitting PDFs and phenomological studies, before discussing potential future extensions, such as incorporating nonlinear evolution equations and PDFs estimated from experimental data. The underlying code of 'pdf4lhc' is now publicly available, offering a valuable tool and resource for researchers worldwide. The distinctive features of 'pdf4lhc' are highlighted, along with the raw code, on its dedicated website at [www.pdf4lhc.org](http://www.pdf4lhc.org). The potential applications and future developments of 'pdf4lhc' are also explored, such as incorporating nonlinear evolution equations, PDFs estimated from experimental data, and PDF fitting fitting with additional parameters, before concluding and summarizing the paper's key findings. The underlying motivation and need for 'pdf4lhc' are explained through a compelling example, involving the calculation of predicted cross-sections for composite processes, involving the integration of multiple contributions from various sources, before discussing the technical challenges and proposed solutions for achieving this goal. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. A key advantage of VRE is its versatility, as it can be integrated with multiple experience replay strategies, including uniform sampling and neural density estimation. A basic implementation of VRE accelerates policy optimization, while a more advanced version surpasses benchmark methods for challenging system control tasks. Moreover, the variance-based experience replay framework presents a straightforward, numerically computable variance estimate that can serve as a reward function. This simplification facilitates policy optimization in systems where the underlying system dynamics are difficult to analyze directly. The VRE method also facilitates policy optimization in systems where the underlying system dynamics are difficult to analyze directly, by serving as a reward function. This is demonstrated on a challenging system control task, in both simulated and real-world settings. The code for this research is available on reasonable request. A simplified variant of the VRE experience replay framework is openly accessible on https://github.com/QianLi-UIUC/VRE-ER. A more advanced code version is available on reasonable request. The MultiTalk Dataset is a large-scale, diverse collection of written English text, encompassing over 20 categories of domains with nearly 1 million dialog turns. This dataset surpasses previous benchmarks in scope, incorporating datasets like ConvAI2, AI2 by a significant margin. Our research presents a novel approach, MultiTalk-LL, that leverages both generative and discriminative models to achieve top performance in conversational dialog tasks. This approach utilizes large language models as pre-trained models, surpassing existing baselines by a considerable margin of 10.3 in ConvAI2's metric F1-score. Our research also introduces two challenging datasets, MultiTalk-Simple and MultiTalk-Complex, consisting of simplified and complex dialog turns respectively, along with their corresponding labels. These datasets provide valuable resources for evaluating model performance in understanding conversational dialog. Our code and datasets are available for public use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/MultiTalk. This achievement is conditional upon certain limitations like model size, while our research also presents comparative analyses of various models, exploring their capabilities in conversational dialog. This includes a head-to-head comparison of LLaMA and T5-3.3, highlighting the potential of both models in this domain. Our findings highlight the vast potential of MultiTalk Dataset in evaluating models' ability to engage in conversational dialog. This research was made possible with the support of a Google AI Research Scholarship, thanks to which we had the opportunity to work on this project full-time for three months. This scholarship also granted us access to Google's internal models, along with guidance from experienced researchers in the field. Our heartfelt appreciation goes out to them for the invaluable support and expertise they shared with us. This work is a modified version of the scholarship project report, with additional research and findings included. Our MultiTalk-LL model has been successfully applied to a related task, namely generating accurate summary notes of conversational dialog, a challenge that has persisted for decades. This is because generating accurate summary notes of a conversation relies heavily on a deep comprehension of the conversation's underlying meaning, a complex task even for humans. Consequently, this has made conversational summarization one of the most difficult applications of natural language processing. Our approach, MultiTalk-LL, leverages both generative and discriminative models to achieve the highest accuracy to date in conversational summarization, a milestone we have achieved conditionally upon certain limitations like model size. This research is a modified version of the scholarship project report, with additional research and findings included.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is designed to be highly adaptable, enabling easy integration with existing codes and allowing users to easily modify its features, making it an invaluable resource for the cosmological community. The full code is available for download at [www.cosmologram.org](http://www.cosmologram.org). The associated papers can be found at [arXiv:1809.02507](http://arxiv.org/abs/1809.02507), [arXiv:1901.06980](http://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06980), and [arXiv:1909.07846](http://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07846). The simulated data sets constructed as part of this research will be hosted in the cosmological repository known as cosmologram, situated at [www.cosmologram.org](http://www.cosmologram.org). Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We establish they are invariant under multiple SLE driven by the Dyson model and the Bru-Wishart process, respectively. Furthermore, we discover that multiple SLE with these driving processes evolves in time on domains that have the same pairings as the imaginary surfaces defined by Miller and Sheffield. This leads to a broader understanding of the relationship between Gaussian free fields, stochastic processes like the Dyson model, and multiple SLE. Additionally, we derive domain evolution equations that are invariant under multiple SLE driven by the Dyson model and the Bru-Wishart process, yielding pairings of Gaussian free fields with multiple marked Brownian motion and multiple SLE with a winding parameter, respectively. Finally, we obtain multiple SLE with a winding parameter as limits of multiple SLE with a variable clustering parameter. This provides an alternative to the approach taken by the work of the January 2020 conference on multiple SLE. We employ the statistical mechanics formalism to derive multiple SLE as limits of lattice models, using the Potts model and the 6-vertex model as examples. This gives rise to multiple SLE with a winding parameter as these limits are taken. We offer multiple SLE with a variable clustering parameter as an intermediate step in obtaining these limits. Consequently, we establish a broader class of stochastic processes that evolve in time on domains that are invariant under multiple SLE. This includes the Dyson model, the Bru-Wishart process, multiple SLE with a winding parameter, and the Potts model and 6-vertex model as examples. Ultimately, we obtain multiple SLE with a winding parameter as limits of lattice models, using the Potts model and the 6-vertex model as instances. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame model that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this model, it is linearized and represented through the use of the Hilbert transform. To apply it to the jet flame scenario, it is assumed that the flame can be represented by a one-dimensional, laminar, premixed flame model that has a known response to an oscillating velocity. By combining the linearized flame model with the surrounding environment, it is possible to represent the variables associated with the jet flame as part of a closed system that can be solved using the Hilbert transform. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In addition, an algorithm has been created to find the minimum number of nodes necessitated for an edge-free representation, and an even more challenging problem is addressed by splitting nodes on a 2-tier bipartite graph visualization, with the goal of removing edge crossings without splitting more than a prescribed number of nodes, where the aim is either to reach an edge-free representation or determine if it is possible to do so with the given node limit. The proposed approach is demonstrated through an illustrative example and also serves as a preliminary step for another challenge discussed in this paper, which involves prioritizing node splittings based on additional attributes or weights. The developed approach has been tested on real-world datasets and compares favorably to existing solutions in terms of solution quality, while offering additional advantages of its own. The introduced approach has its own limitations, yet the paper also presents an alternative algorithmic possibility called the "reverse" approach that could serve as a benchmark for comparison with the proposed solution. The paper's contributions consist of both practical applications (e.g. splitting node in Wikipedia's infobox) and theoretical value (e.g. planarity testing in 2-tier bipartite graphs). The paper's findings offer implications for the visualization of relationships between distinct groups of objects, even in cases where relationships themselves are not the primary subject of interest, but rather they are connected objects, and provides an empirical evaluation of the proposed approach through real-world datasets, in addition to an in-depth analysis of its theoretical value. The paper's value also lies in its practical usefulness, its simplicity, and its ability to serve as foundation for more challenging problems, as well as its unique set of features that differentiates it from other graph visualization methods, due in part to the constraints it imposes on the underlying graph structure, by limiting the number of node splittings. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. We also discuss the scope for enhancing this design's performance through future laser technology and higher-power signal modulation. Moreover, this design can be used to enhance the sensitivity of existing Michelson setups, such as LIGO and Virgo, by modifying their recycling systems. We demonstrate the sloshing Sagnac design's effectiveness in detecting binary neutron star merger waves with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10, achieving a milestone that even the most sophisticated future detectors will find difficult to surpass. We have made the design's documentation and simulation code publicly available as part of the LIGO Algorithm Library. The potential of this innovative design has significant implications for the optimization of existing and future gravitational wave detectors in the high-frequency range. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. We found that this gate design maintains considerable frequency stability, especially when the gap frequency is low, and that the required laser power remains reasonably restrained, making this design suitable for practical applications with actual trapped ion setups. Additionally, an error correction algorithm is developed to accurately calculate the minimum required duration of Molmer-Sorensen gates, and we present simulation results to facilitate easy adaptation to new chain configurations. This research demonstrates the feasibility of implementing robust Molmer-Sorensen gates within experimental setups of trapped ions, and the associated tools can be easily modified to accommodate other entangling gates based on standing waves. Ultimately, this scheme facilitates the creation of quantum gates with inherent frequency immunity, an indispensable feature for reliable operation in real-world setups, and the developed framework is fully customizable for a wide range of entangling gates and chain configurations. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Our code has been made publicly accessible on https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. They further explored related statistics on nested structures within skew Dyck paths and skew standard tableaux. By connecting marked trees to branching processes, they interpreted their results in terms of survival probabilities in these processes. A notable finding showed that among all marked trees with the same number of nodes, only a minuscule fraction have exactly one deepest node, with this fraction diminishing quickly as the number of nodes increases. In the context of standard tableaux, their findings demonstrated that the majority of deepest nodes are located at the end of the sequence, with the exception of staircase tableaux. They demonstrated that the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees can be represented as a sum of independent, identically distributed variables, which enabled them to calculate this sum's standard deviation as the number of nodes increases. Through the connection to branching processes, they found that the ratio of the number of descendants to the number of ancestors in these processes converges to $\frac53$ in the limiting case, which they felt deserved greater attention as a standalone result. This limit result, they pointed out, differs from the ratio in the original Galton-Watson branching process, which converges to a value of $1$ if the process is to survive. They emphasized that this $\frac53$ value is significant because it represents the average number of nodes that an individual in the population will move towards during each generation, rather than the number of offspring an individual has. This distinction led them to rephrase this limit result as the solution to a nonlinear equation, which they further generalized to the $n$th power, obtaining the relation $S^n=s$ as the number of nodes increases without bound, where $s$ and $S$ are the limits of the average number of descendants and the number of descendants per ancestor, respectively. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the widespread adoption of energy storage systems in the future, understanding this phenomenon could be crucial for developing strategies to minimize storage units' risk aversion and ensure long-term grid stability. Key findings also provide practical value for electricity market operators and utility companies looking to manage energy storage units effectively. Finally, our research highlights the necessity for new risk management frameworks that can adapt to the changing nature of energy storage systems and their operational risks. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that a careful analysis of storage units' risk aversion is necessary to ensure secure and reliable grid operations in the future. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. Our findings highlight the significance of examining both mesoscopic and larger-sized samples when investigating the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells. Furthermore, this study provides a straightforward approach for exploring neutral states in HgTe quantum wells by adjusting the size of the samples rather than the width of the quantum wells. This approach is crucial for achieving reliable energy gaps and neutral state formation in this material. Our research reveals that a reliable energy gap can be achieved in HgTe quantum wells despite the uncertainty associated with this parameter, and also demonstrates that the condition required for neutral state formation is much more stringent than initially anticipated, thus emphasizing the importance of examining both transport and magnetotransport properties thoroughly. A comprehensive model has been proposed to explain the resistant oscillations observed in larger-sized samples, and demonstrates that heavy hole landau levels serve as a reservoir that affects the transport properties of these samples significantly. Finally, this study has been accompanied by a review of the current understanding of HgTe quantum wells, focusing on both transport and magnetotransport properties, and also discusses theoretical models used to describe this material's energy spectrum. Our examination of transport properties also uncovered the presence of a stable, positive resistance emerging in the range of low-magnetic-field conditions, and was found to be associated with the formation of helical edge states in HgTe quantum wells. Our research has been carried out using a home-built, magnetoresistance apparatus, and has been supplemented by a discussion of the apparatus's design along with the techniques used to prepare the samples. Ultimately, this study has been a preliminary step towards a comprehensive examination of non-equilibrium superconductivity in HgTe quantum wells driven by strong light-matter interaction. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning cells independent TDD modes, followed by a non-cooperative game determining transmission modes, but carefully managing the cut-off metric to prevent interference and ensure fairness. Numerical studies under real-world scenarios reveal significant improvements in network efficiency, with dynamic TDD outperforming traditional TDD by as much as 2.5 in terms of throughput-to-user-density ratio. We've also analyzed the effects of varying traffic patterns and network density on dynamic TDD's effectiveness. We've further adapted this approach for coherent TDD networks, avoiding cross-cell interference and coherent TDD's associated challenges. Overall, our dynamic TDD solution provides a versatile, adaptable, and efficient solution for emerging, densely populated networks. We've implemented this solution in an open-source framework for ubiquitous TDMA, serving as a starting point for further optimization in specific network contexts. In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Additionally, our approach demonstrates the ability to efficiently optimize natural language processing models for the SuperGLUE benchmark, achieving comparable performance at significantly reduced cost. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghdng/hamiltone. We believe that this simple, efficient, and versatile method will serve as a valuable baseline for the community in this emerging field of research. As an aside, our investigation into the relationship between meta-learning and the choice of activation function reveals that ReLU leads to poor generalization, a discovery we feel warrants further examination from the perspective of both meta-learning and the broader machine learning community. Furthermore, our attempt at applying this method to hyperparameter optimization for the number of layers in a model through neural architecture search proved promising and opened up related research questions for us, leaving behind a usable codebase at https://github.com/ghdng/sas. We propose two particular research paths that we feel merit exploration in the future: the potential of substituting current neural network architectures with graph neural networks, which we believe would result in enhanced performance, as well as the possible extension of our method to a more general hyperparameter optimization framework through neural architecture search. We have made the code for both projects open-source and they can be found at https://github.com/ghdng/hamiltone and https://github.com/ghdng/sas respectively. We firmly believe that our findings, accompanied by the accessible code, will facilitate further advancement in this area of research. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Additionally, our results demonstrate that this framework is effective across various machine learning models, including both linear and deep learning-based ones, and can be operated with different reliability metrics. We also present an application of this system to enhancing the safety of self-driving cars by correcting a simulation-based dataset. This leads to a significant reduction in false negatives and an increase in true positives in detecting critical scenarios. We make the code and datasets available for public use.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, an evaluation of augmented training data using a high-degree of gloss definitions per context indicates that increasing the number of definitions per context leads to a decrease in WSD performance.  Ultimately, this study validates the broad applicability of BERT in WSD tasks across multiple sources, while providing useful insights for future research in this area.  The proposed approach has been successfully tested on the SenseVal2019 benchmark, yielding performance improvements over baseline models.  The code and models developed in this study have been made publicly available on GitHub.  Future work is suggested to explore the integration of BERT-based WSD models with embedded knowledge structures, as well as evaluations using more rigorous approaches, such as the F$_1$-score for the three-way classification task.  Ultimately, this study demonstrates the viability of using BERT in conjunction with semantic knowledge to efficiently address the WSD challenge. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the top quark charge was confirmed to be $2.748 \pm 0.461$. The research paved the way for further studies of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions and nutured analyses of heavy quark formation in quark-gluon plasma. The findings were further supported by re-analyzing 0.58 inverse nanobarns of LHC proton-proton data at a 7 TeV center-of-mass energy, where the measured cross-section for top quark pairs was 162 nanobarns with a 22 nanobarns uncertainty. The smaller sample showed an improved sensitivity, allowing the determination of the top quark charge as $2.85 \pm 0.45$. The results from both experiments met the signals expected from models proposing that top quarks might have anomalous charges, with the magnitude of deviations from standard model predictions found to be less than 0.75 for the proton-proton data and less than 0.46 for the proton-lead data. This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. This work is pertinent to domains such as recommendation systems and medical diagnosis graphs. This paper is an expanded version of a workshop paper that was previously published. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Lastly, our formalism has the potential to be extended to fermionic systems and more intricate configurations. It is particularly well-suited for modeling open quantum systems and investigating the behavior of atomic gases in optimal traps or similar configurations with confined regions. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Experimental findings confirm our proposed approach yields superior outcomes than conventional methods, largely due to the increased reliability it affords. Our study hopes to stimulate further research into the widespread application of j-k fold CV across machine learning contexts. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. Moreover, we found that the shape of the absorption profile can be utilized as an indicator of saturation, offering an alternative to other established methods. If appropriate corrections are applied, this shape can be utilized to calibrate the number of atoms accurately, even in scenarios where other parameters, such as fluorescence signals or kinetic temperatures, are difficult to determine reliably. Our findings are particularly significant for strontium, a highly sensitive element with low absorption levels, but our model can be easily extended to other elements and atoms. Our research provides a clear understanding of the behavior of absorption patterns in ultracold gases and reveals their hidden information content. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for a nuanced understanding of the relationships between stress, volume fraction, and viscosity in the complex and dynamic process of shear thickening. Human-made materials like polymers and colloids will also benefit from this research, as it highlights the pivotal role that microscale interactions play in governing the viscosity of these materials, even when subjected to significant stresses. The development of a universal function also highlights the limitations of using the concept of yield stress in describing these materials, as it represents an "intermediate state of confusion" that arises from the Einstein's relation, where the combination of zero shear viscosity and shear stress at zero shear rate yield the same value, yet through different physical mechanisms. Consequently, any change in shear stress will result in a change in viscosity, leading to a constant ratio, and thus, a fixed position along the universal curve, independent of the applied stress. The overall significance of this research is underscored by the fact that, despite being discovered over a century ago, the fundamental physics governing the relationship between stress and volume fraction in dense mixtures remains not fully comprehended, and thus, this work offers a substantial contribution to the existing body of knowledge. The primary methodology employed in this study involved subjecting a dense and monodisperse suspension of silica spheres in glycerol to varying levels of stress through particle-level mechanical interactions, coupled with high-speed imaging to measure the resulting particle velocities and distances between them. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study's implications for public administration's ethical guidelines and the potential for training programmes in Web search literacy are discussed. Moreover, it is crucial that these professionals are empowered to make informed judgments that are not unduly influenced by search algorithms. This study paves the way for further empirical research on Web search's impact on professional knowledge work in other sectors. It is also crucial that developers of search engines take certain measures, such as making search algorithms' biases more transparent and providing options to reduce them. This is particularly important for professional users who rely heavily on Web search for their assessment. This is an original study conducted in Sri Lanka with a sample of 30 government officials, but its findings are relevant to a broader context. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Optimized reconstruction parameters for this method include a resolution of $4.5mm^3$ and a temporal regularization of $10^{-4}$. This technique also facilitates feasible data compression with minimal reduction in image quality. A comparison with conventional MRI techniques, including contrast agent-induced changes, showed no significant differences. This method has the added benefit of eliminating the need for manual segmentation of tumors and organs due to natural alignment of images with deformable transformation, thus reducing overall treatment planning time by at least 20%. A study with ten subjects over multiple sessions revealed no significant difference in image quality, thus making this method suitable for long-term monitoring of changes, such as tumor growth. A limitation of this method is the presence of artifacts in high-sensitivity acquisitions, particularly in the ventral direction, though this can be minimized with modified sampling patterns, such as SENSE-based rCASPR, which reduces artifacts by filtering out certain respiratory phases. This method has the potential for wide application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI due to its high-quality images, small scan duration, low contrast variability, minimal tumor segmentation time, suitability for long-term monitoring of changes

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Moreover, we've made this exact algorithm's source code available for others to use. This can be particularly beneficial for large-scale NLP systems where a substantial amount of time is typically wasted on Monte Carlo approximation calculations. We've further demonstrated the efficacy of our exact algorithm by incorporating it into the evaluation of the BART simple transformer model on the SNLI dataset, a commonly used benchmark. We've also undertaken an in-depth examination of the factors that influence the computational time required for paired-permutation tests. This is crucial for enabling optimal use of our exact algorithm in different settings. Finally, we've introduced the notion of a ``effective sample size'' (ESS) to provide a more precise, scalable way of measuring the computational time required for paired-permutation tests. This ESS metric can be utilized to guide practical decisions when evaluating the statistical significance of NLP system performance. We've made all source codes and datasets used in this research study available for others to use. This enables replication of our results and facilitates the further improvement of paired-permutation testing algorithms. This research was funded by the SNLI Exact WMTP Testing Award and the Google Faculty Research Award, both of which are highly prestigious and competitive grants in the NLP community. This research has been supported by grants from Google and unknown other sources, both of which are leading funders of NLP research. This feedback was extremely valuable in helping us refine this research. We'd also like to thank Qunhua Song, Yansong Zhao, and Liang James Lee for offering their insights on this research. Lastly, we'd like to thank the PA permutation testing algorithm developers for creating this essential tool that enabled us to develop and test our own exact WMTP

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, it is shown that each loom space can be characterized by a unique veering triangulation, establishing a bijective relationship between loom spaces and veering triangulations up to topological equivalence. Furthermore, this equivalence allows for the direct translation of veering triangulation properties into corresponding characteristics of its associated loom space. Lastly, it is proved that the group associated with a loom space is topologically invariant and that this property enables the extension of Thurston's Topological Rigidity Theorem to a broader spectrum of veering triangulations. Consequently, it is possible to apply the theorem to a broader range of groups, including those whose action on hyperbolic planes is not planar. Ultimately, this research expands the scope of the classical Fock-Sigurina theorem by encompassing a more diverse array of groups. It is noteworthy that this research was conceived during the author's graduate studies at the University of Virginia, supervised by the renowned topologist Richard Kent. Focal points of this dissertation are reflected in the advancement of veering theory, the sophisticated properties of loom spaces, and the rigorous application of topological rigidity to a diverse and previously inaccessible category of groups. Ultimately, it demonstrates the groups with which which hyperbolic planes are not invariant can be accurately described as those whose associated veering triangulations exhibit a specific property dubbed "twisted tubes". Consequently, this research successfully expands the parameters of the Fock-Sigurina theorem by providing a more inclusive classification of groups deemed "geometrically finite". Ultimately, this classification is equivalent to those groups whose action on hyperbolic planes is planar, thus solidifying the foundation for this expanded theorem. It is the hope of the author that this research will give rise to a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate relationship between topology and geometry. Ultimately, it is the author's conviction that the innovative applications demonstrated in this study will pave the way for the further advancement of veering theory and related topological disciplines. It is the genuine desire of the author to express their most sincere and heartfelt gratitude to their graduate program supervisor, the distinguished topologist Richard Kent, for providing invaluable guidance, encouragement, and mentor

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. It is evident from recent market fluctuations how news headlines and cryptocurrency prices are affected. This research paper presents an ensemble of state-of-the-art techniques to forecast stock prices. It starts with applying a BERT-based sentiment analysis model to analyze the emotional state of Apple Inc investors listed on NASDAQ. A subsequent GAN-based model predicts the company's stock price based on technical indicators, global stock indexes, commodity prices, and historical prices along with the sentiment scores. This model's performance is compared to benchmark models including LSTM, GRU, vanilla GAN, and ARIMA. It achieves the lowest MAE and SSE among all compared models. Furthermore, an intrinsic value model is introduced to enhance the GAN model's performance by scaling the predicted stock prices. It outperforms the benchmark models in terms of both performance indicators in 80% of the data samples. This research paper also applies the model to forecast Microsoft Corp stock prices with the same indicators except for technical indicators. It utilizes historical stock prices, sentiment analysis, and commodity prices. The results show that the GAN model achieves the lowest MAE and SSE among all compared models in 90% of the data samples. It is noteworthy that ARIMA model performs better in 10% of the data samples. It is also demonstrated that the model can forecast stock prices listed on other exchanges including NASDAQ, NYSE, and SPX 500 index. It is worth mentioning that the model fails to forecast cryptocurrency prices listed on major exchanges such as Bitcoin. It is also demonstrated that the model can forecast commodity prices listed on exchanges such as gold and oil prices. It is also capable of forecasting various economic indicators such as inflation rates and unemployment rates in the United States. It is also capable of forecasting stock market indices listed on exchanges such as S\&P 500, NASDAQ, and NYSE. It is also capable of forecasting stock prices of technology companies listed on exchanges such as Apple

We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We propose a strategy for future experiments to combine the limits from searches for single and double Higgs boson productions in electron-positron collisions. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This approach allowed us to estimate the drag experienced by the cylinder in both orientations with a reasonable degree of accuracy. We also used it to interpret the results of our experiments and those of others. This approach could be used to estimate the drag experienced by other solid objects moving through granular materials. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Furthermore, an almost identical pattern of reduced $v_3$ in comparison to $v_2$ holds true across various centrality levels, despite initial geometry's influence being accounted for. Nonetheless, once the influence of colliding midrapidity target sides is removed, we observed an enhancement in $v_3$ over $v_2$ in the most central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Our analysis suggests that initial anisotropic geometry explains a significant portion of observed triangular flow, yet other factors, such as particle production dynamics, also play a crucial role. Our results also demonstrate that triangular flow, like elliptical flow, adheres to a specific scaling based on charged particle multiplicity. Finally, our findings show that midrapidity initial anisotropic geometry is largely driven by colliding target sides in the most central collisions. Our research offers theoretical evidence for experimental observations of increased $J/ψ$ production in heavy ion collisions and initial state geometry's influence on proton interferometry parameters. Our results also demonstrate that the duration of heavy ion collisions' formation time is significantly less than collision duration, our most critical contribution thus far. Our research has implications for future experiments and provides a solid foundation for further investigation into specific aspects of heavy ion collisions, such as the behavior of strange quarks and photons. Our initial anisotropic geometry research has been applied to proton-like ion and lead ion collisions. Our results demonstrate that heavy ion collisions' formation time is indeed shorter than collision duration, our most critical contribution thus far. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. Specifically, it reviews outstanding results from data samples collected at 7 TeV, 8 TeV, 13 TeV, and 13 TeV + 36 TeV center-of-mass energies, featuring enhanced precision in measuring the CP-violating process in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ and landmark measurements in rare processes like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$. These discoveries position the ATLAS experiment at the forefront of rare B-meson decay research and demonstrate the potential of the LHC to explore rare occurrences of CP non-conservation in the weak interaction with unprecedented precision. This research paves the way for further investigations at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, which are anticipated to significantly enhance the statistical confidence of these measurements by factors of 4 to 10. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the proposed method is showcased through numerical experiments for two renowned PDEs, namely the one-dimensional Burgers equation and the two-dimensional Allen-Cahn equation. Furthermore, the impact of different iteration control strategies on the preservation of properties is visually depicted and quantified. The results show that the modified flexible generalised minimum residual iteration, when employed with a 20,000-degree polynomial system from the Burgers equation, is capable of maintaining property preservation while achieving an impressive level of accuracy of 10^-6. The corresponding data is available at the associated repository. The proposed method offers significant potential for preserving physical properties in numerical solutions of various PDEs, especially those requiring the solution of large nonlinear systems of equations. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, even in real-time. The network's efficiency enables real-time application on desktop computers without the need for graphics processing units. The proposed method demonstrates accurate results in multiple difficult cases, outperforming conventional approaches based on Laplace Belbel Belal optimisation, and has the potential to integrate with various navigation systems for real-time soft-tissue matching in laparoscopic surgery. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We anticipate that this benchmark and accompanying methods will contribute to the progress of self-supervised flow estimation, an intricate problem that requires further research. Our code and datasets are available at: \url{https://github.com/MastonT/3d_scene_flow_benchmark}.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate with superior efficiency, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the versatility of artificial neural networks with the operational efficiency of spiking neural networks, achieving a substantial reduction in computational demands. As an example, our research shows that using a Random Neural Network can reduce the computational load of Inception V1 by 50 times and MobileNet by 20 times, all while maintaining or improving classification accuracy. In addition to its computational efficiency, our proposed method also offers other benefits, including simplified training, enhanced robustness, and the ability to effectively handle classification problems involving incomplete information. We have made the associated code and models publicly available, and our research demonstrates particular potential in optimizing real-world AI networks like Inception V1 and MobileNet V2. Our findings also demonstrate how to efficiently classify integromolecular reactions based on chemical properties, achieving a precision of 81.8% when classifying 100% of reactions correctly, and 85.1% when classifying 90% of reactions correctly, both with only 10% of the original feature set. This breakthrough discovery enables us to tackle big data sets that were previously too large for even the most advanced AI networks, and we have made significant progress in this area by successfully applying this method to large data sets consisting of millions of entries. Our research has significant implications for AI networks in general, and we have made the associated code and models publicly available. Our aim is to contribute to the wider community of AI researchers and practitioners by providing them with this free tool, and we look forward to collaborating with them to build upon this foundation. Our methodology has been validated through extensive testing on diverse benchmark datasets, and we are confident that it is a fundamental breakthrough that is applicable to a broad range of classification tasks across various domains. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. By employing the entropy density, we determined the specific heat capacity, susceptibility, and other relevant thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter. Additionally, we calculated the causal speed of sound and the condition for causality in spin-polarized strange quark stars. By analyzing the equation of state, we obtained numerical results for spin-polarized strange quark stars, including their mass-radius curves, and compared these with other studies. By evaluating the free energy density, we determined the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter at finite temperature and magnetic field strength. Finally, we examined the impact of the bag constant, strange quark mass, and electromagnetic pressure on the structure and density of spin-polarized strange quark stars. This research provides explicit expressions for the temperature and magnetic field dependences of the speed of sound, causal speed of sound, and density of spin-polarized strange quark stars. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the PMH-property is not necessary for a cubic graph to satisfy the E2F condition, albeit not serving as a necessary condition. Consequently, we categorize the papillon graphs as a distinct class of cubic graphs that are distinct from the known classes, namely genus one graphs, orientable double cover graphs, and bi-cubic graphs. Our research also reveals that the papillon graph has a large genus, specifically genus 4, which remains uncategorized within the known classes of cubic graphs. Our work on the papillon graph provides an infinite generation of cubic graphs with specific properties, expanding the limited existing body of research on infinite families of cubic graphs parameterized by integer values. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Ultimately, this system call learning technique is its own filter generator, thereby offering a substantial amount of versatility. This project's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/CMU-NRSL/timeloops.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed filter algorithm. Furthermore, the integration of the filter with a model-based sensor management framework is illustrated through simulations of target detection, where the algorithm is shown to efficiently identify targets within a region of interest by adjusting the sensors' positions, according to various configurations tested. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of winning. Experimental results on a large-scale simulated soccer environment show our approach outperforms traditional policy networks and conventional strategies like shooting often and defending rarely. Furthermore, by conducting feature importance analysis, we reveal several actionable insights: defending is generally the best action in critical situations; the preference for attacking actions changes throughout the game; and there is an optimal time to take corners, throw-ins, and free kicks. Our code is available at https://github.com/TianXiaoDxj/RRSLZFB.

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).
