A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. Additionally, the investigation found that this model accurately predicts statistical measures, such as Reynolds stress and turbulent kinetic energy, from low-resolution data across various Reynolds numbers with a high degree of accuracy. It is worthwhile noting that the model's capability to recreate pressure patterns required the addition of a residual generation network. The findings of this study demonstrate the efficacy of this deep learning framework in predicting high-resolution turbulent velocity patterns and associated statistical measures from limited data across a wide range of Reynolds numbers, with potential applications in the simulation of turbulent flows. The model's effectiveness is attributed to its specially designed multiscale architecture that enables it to accurately predict high-resolution velocity patterns and associated statistical measures from low-resolution data at different Reynolds numbers. It is also emphasized that the use of Markov chain theory helped optimize the model's performance by decreasing the number of model parameters required. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. We've openly sourced L2Explorer, along with accompanying resources, to foster significant advances in lifelong learning research.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. Leveraging this methodology, we demonstrate the capabilities of DCR graphs in uncovering processes and analytically examine its precision guarantees, showing that it yields precise temporal processes in ninety-nine percent of cases. Our approach simplifies process discovery, utilizing minimal data, yet remaining robust in the face of process changes, making it a versatile and ever-adaptable solution. Our approach and associated test data are available online at https://processmining.github.io/examples/. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ProcessMining/. Our research is an initial step towards a broader goal, aiming to develop a suite of process discovery tools, capable of efficiently uncovering underlying processes from raw data, efficiently handling process changes, and providing actionable insights for process improvement, available online at https://processmining.github.io/. Our approach builds upon our previous work, published in Lopes, Propp, De Weerdt, and Aalders, 2022, which uncovered processes from static data, but not addressing the need for process models to adapt over time. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. It starts with a detailed explanation of why and how Griffiths' vision of using transcendental methods for rationality testing and variety compactification arose. Subsequent sections explore three specific applications: (1) using Hodge-theoretic methods to prove the irreducibility of the moduli space of curves with a distinguished point, (2) discussing Deligne-Oort's work on the moduli space of abelian varieties with complex multiplication, and (3) examining how Mumford's work on the moduli space of curves with a divisor of certain type led to a rationality test. Finally, possible future directions are outlined. Notably, possible extensions to higher dimensions and the role of intermediate Jacobians are also discussed. This document is based on a talk given at the 2017 Summer Meeting of the Southeastern International Number Theory Conference.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Additionally, due to the narrower NUV$-r$ color indicator, the same trends were not observed when analyzing the U$-H$ color. Hence, more specific measures of star formation are necessary for a more comprehensive understanding of the relation. Moreover, the research revealed that the NUV$-r$ color of the central region dominates the color of the outer region in the UV-optical color U$-r$. Consequently, a combination of both NUV$-r$ and U$-r$ colors would offer an even more precise method of examining the relation between star formation and galaxy mass. The current study provides a foundation for future work involving larger galaxy samples and the application of similar methods using different color indicators. If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The code of the proposed system has been made available open-source on GitHub.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. Nevertheless, we are able to prove that this time period can be delayed when compared to the undissipated transport equation. The approach used to solve this problem involves combining the characteristics method with the Bukreysham-Holland technique and the properties of the Maximal $H^{3}$ space. The research also expands the scope of previous works addressing the transport equation with fractional decay. The relationship between this equation and the two-component Camassa-Holm system is explored in the study, demonstrating that the later system's well-posedness issues arise specifically from the non-local flow rather than the decay term. The paper also provides an example where the solution's singularity can be precisely determined based on the value of $\alpha$, indicating that the time period required for the solution to develop a singularity or smoothness can be explicitly calculated when the initial conditions are known precisely. The research further shows that the solution's decay rates are related to the values of $\alpha$ and $\kappa$. The study also examines and extends the transport equation's properties by incorporating the BMO space, thereby enabling the investigation of the well-posedness of the equation when the solution's decay rates are unknown. The paper's innovations lay the groundwork for further studying similar transport equations featuring non-local properties and decay terms. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Finally, possible sizes in ternary GCM quadruples are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 42x42 and a few scattered instances. Prior works on Golay complementary arrays focused primarily on two-dimensional spaces. Given the scarcity of 4-D Golay complementary arrays, we propose a decay model predicting the decrease of GCA frequencies when moving from a lower dimension. It is also demonstrated that the majority of low-dimensional Golay complementary arrays have a repeating pattern concerning their block size and number of elements per block. We have made the code for our research projects publicly available on https://github.com/yangzw93/GCAConstruct. This code enables users to generate binary GCM pairs for sizes 16x16, 20x20, 24x24, 32x32, 40x40, 56x56, 60x60, 64x64, 78x78, ternary GCM pairs for sizes 6x6, 14x14, 18x18, 22x22, 26x26, 30x30, 34x34, 38x38, 42x42, and quaternary GCM pairs for sizes 4x4, 8x8, 12x12, 16x16, 20x20, 24x24, 28x28, 32x32, 36x36, 40x40. We have successfully constructed multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays in spaces up to 4-D and for array sizes up to 78x78, using our newly introduced method which leverages ring identities. This research paves the way for an in-depth analysis of omni-directional precoding techniques in 4-D spaces

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon. 
Ultimately, this research paves the way for addressing quantum coherences with coupled atoms in silicon by precisely placed dopants, empowering both large-scale quantum computations and quantum simulations in silicon. 
The results demonstrated in this study are particularly related to phosphorus in silicon, however they are generally applicable to other coupled atom systems with a significant exchange interaction in the quantum tunneling regime. 
The exchange interaction can be further refined through the use of donor shape resonance states, a phenomenon that arises from valley interference and envelope anisotropy, however it is essential to recognize that this interaction is inherently robust, maintaining both its magnitude and variability when considering different donor arrays. 
Ultimately, this robust exchange interaction, combined with precise placement of dopants, can be utilized to address individual coupled atoms in silicon with both silicon and electron spin resonance, empowering both large-scale quantum computations and quantum simulations in silicon.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a further contribution, the GP 2 compiler source code is being made available to the research community through an open-source licence.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. As the algorithm's specifications can be adjusted, it comes with a user-guide to ensure seamless integration into various projects, and we anticipate its potential usefulness in large-scale categorical data analysis. As an example of its versatility, we demonstrate the proposed method's capability to handle overlapping clusters of variables by modifying the algorithm to employ the Fused Lasso, resulting in a more detailed and highly interpretable model when analyzing the Amazon product review dataset. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks and genres. However, the effectiveness of these models can be limited when processing specific domains like scientific text, where they lack initial knowledge. To overcome this, we propose a method that efficiently incorporates structured knowledge from knowledge graphs into large language models, leveraging specific relation-based knowledge that enhances the models' understanding. Our approach differs from conventional approaches that utilize natural language sentences with embedded knowledge and offers substantial advantages in terms of data efficiency and a shift in inductive bias. Our method successfully applies this approach to LLMs for natural language generation and our experimental results on the T5 and FLAN frameworks demonstrate significant improvements (22-42%) in generation tasks when using our method in place of conventional knowledge infusion. Additionally, we find that this method can be effective at a much lower data scale (only 20% of the original required scale) and yields comparable performance to traditional knowledge infusion at full data scale. Our approach has a particular benefit for low-resource generation tasks, where large text datasets are difficult to obtain, and thus, our method presents a promising direction for incorporating external knowledge to enhance the performance of unsupervised generation tasks. Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps. Our scheme has been implemented as an open-source project on GitHub, available for public use. Our research demonstrates that this simple two-triangle algorithm can be adapted for different resolutions, platform variations, and specific rendering requirements, making it a versatile solution. Our data and algorithm are freely accessible at https://github.com/TencentVRP/SimpleAntiAliasing. Our scheme has been published in a paper that is part of the proceedings of the VRPC 2020 conference held in Shenzhen, China. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Moreover, successful applications of tiny models like DPCRN have paved the way for further research in the utilization of dual-path RNNs and Convolution Recurrent Networks in the speech processing domain. The DPCRN model code has been made available through the GitHub platform.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. Even when evaluating conditions far from those originally tested, the model retains a high level of accuracy with a mean error of less than 10% in predicting the total heat transfer in relation to the predicted value. Furthermore, the model's ability to preserve the precise scaling of the thermal boundary layer thickness across various forcing levels, even when these forces vary significantly, demonstrates the robustness of this simple two-fluid model. Despite its computational efficiency, this model exhibits a slightly higher resistance to the development of the characteristic spotty pattern convection becomes, in higher resolution models, due to the absence of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Nonetheless, the model's marginal error of 1.5 Kelvin when solving a standard, widely used convection scheme test case, indicates its potential for use in higher resolution models. The current research showcases the multi-fluid model's capability in accurately simulating convection, even under a highly simplified form, and provides a dynamic framework that can be further developed to improve the representation of convection within modern weather and climate models. The model's future applications will depend on its ability to be integrated with existing models, its computational efficiency, and the associated data requirements, despite already demonstrating a level of scalability comparable to other sophisticated schemes when evaluating large ranges of forcing conditions. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. This similarity exists despite the distinct non-linear YM charge formation in the latter case. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we introduce a method to obtain the Wigner function from an optical tomogram by employing a Gaussian filter that is determined by the state itself, providing a state-dependent approach to reconstruction. Ultimately, our study highlights the intricate interconnection between the optical tomogram, Wigner function, and Wigner-Araki-Sudarshan operator, revealing the inherent properties that dictate reconstruction in quantum optics. 

An important aspect to consider when engaging with this research is the use of a specific phase space representation, namely the positive Wigner function, which significantly simplifies state reconstruction. Nevertheless, this representation comes with the drawback of potentially marking reconstructed states as classically simulable when the actual state corresponds to a non-classical system with a negative Wigner function. An alternative approach using the anti-Wick symbol is also explored and found to yield equivalent results under the same conditions. A notable finding from our investigations revealed that the condition of positive Wigner function holds an $N$-fold periodic structure in the frequency domain, which we termed the "frequency crystal graph," and is deemed a distinctive hallmark of non-classical entanglement in continuous-variable systems. This concept can be utilized to determine the recoverability of a negative Wigner function from the optical tomogram, serving as an indicator for the existence of non-classical effects. Ultimately, this study uncovers novel perspectives on state reconstruction and reveals the intricate relationship between different quantum representations and the underlying physics of continuous-variable systems. It also introduces the "frequency crystal graph" as a novel tool for detecting non-classical entanglement in systems of radiation field.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. In addition, we provide explicit numerical examples to illustrate the performance of this method. This novel approach paves the way for effective application of tensor network methods in the study of complex, dynamic scenarios. Additionally, we successfully recover previous research results on the entanglement entropy in random quantum quench events. This approach also enables the computation of after-quench entanglement scaling, allowing for an examination of the transition from lattice entanglement to continuum coherence. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of this method in investigating post-quench phase transitions by tracing the evolution of entanglement entropy and coherence length with time. This is exemplified through the study of a quantum critical chain undergoing quench fluctuations in its vicinity. We also investigate the permanent disappearance of the gap-free spectrum in the middle phase quench regime and the consequent scaling of the coherence length with time. This is contrasted with the short-time scaling observed in the two phase quench regimes (i.e., pre- and post-equilibrium phases) where the gap-free spectrum initially exhibits power-law scaling with time. We also examine the corresponding time-dependent entanglement entropy saturation values in all quench scenarios. This approach also facilitates an in-depth analysis of post-quench state destruction exponents, which we find to be independent of the chain length in all quench scenarios studied. This includes the investigation of the exponents in all possible post-quench state destruction scenarios, from continuous generation of the gap-free spectrum to its complete disappearance, where we find that these exponents demonstrate no dependence on the chain length. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Our findings also illustrate the advantages of balanced exploration-exploitation schedules, as well as the potential risks of agent knowledge sharing. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhengzw/CoIL. In addition, we introduce a novel evaluation metric, the Imitation Ratio, to assess the purity and reliability of learned behaviors in the absence of guidance. This metric is universally applicable and facilitates uniform assessment of various reinforcement learning methods that leverage inter-agent knowledge transfer. Our research demonstrates significant improvements in using peer agents' experiences through efficient exploration and robust value function filtering, thereby contributing a foundational understanding of the interplay between learning from experience and learning from others in reinforcement learning settings. Our work is relevant to a broad spectrum of applications, including multi-agent systems, where agents learn from each other in complex dynamic environments, such as traffic management, energy trading, and microfinance, among others. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We conclude that search-limited PAC codes are a superior error-correction code architecture for many future memory-constrained applications. We also propose a hybrid PAC code architecture that combines the advantages of convolutional and polar codes, offering lower computations and comparable or improved error-correction performance, making it an attractive solution for future wireless communications systems. We illustrate the merger's performance benefits with an example of the TC-16 standard for the Internet of Things. Finally, we outline potential extensions and variations of search-limited PAC codes, including Trellis-coded PAC codes, Polar-PAC codes, and Hybrid PAC codes. We anticipate these code architectures gaining significance in the design of future low-complexity, high-performance wireless communication systems. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. As an additional contribution, we provide efficient checks for particular variants of snapshot isolation that are specific to MongoDB's transaction protocols. Our approach is valuable for database developers and maintenance teams, allowing them to easily verify the consistency guarantees provided by their database systems, even for complex systems like MongoDB. Our approach was made possible by our development of a general framework for verifying the consistency of snapshot isolation variants against arbitrary predicates. As a testament to the generality of our approach, we successfully applied it to the Elasticsearch transaction protocol, which, unlike MongoDB, provides transactional consistency guarantees in a multi-document scenario. Our framework encompasses multiple variants of snapshot isolation, allowing for efficient checks of specific variants. As an example, we used this framework to efficiently check the consistency of Elasticsearch's transaction protocol, which yields a pseudocode for its protocol. Our approach is suited for large-scale database systems like MongoDB and Elasticsearch, which provide transactional guarantees but lack clear documentation of their transactional protocols. Our approach provides a practical solution for verifying the consistency of such systems, even in the absence of official documentation. Our work has implications for the development of verification tools, emphasizing the importance of clear documentation of database systems, particularly their transactional components. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. Consequently, this simple yet versatile model serves as a relevant and timely an analogy for understanding the dynamics of intricate systems entangled in triangular relationships.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also calculated the total energy required to suspend the solar wind and suspend the plasma oscillations, finding they both needed about 30 Watts per square meter, but with the energy to suspend the plasma oscillations making up only a tiny fraction of the total, while the rest is mainly the energy of the wind itself. We used these results to estimate the total number of solar winds particles reaching the solar surface, which we found to be around 10 to the power of 49 per second, or about 100 times the number of particles reaching the Earth in the same time period, and we also calculated the total number of particles, both free and attached, which we found to be around 10 to the power of 52 per second. We used the data from the close approaches to create detailed computer models of the solar wind distributions, which we validated by comparing the results with the actual data, and we used these models to map the distribution of particles and energy across the surface of the sun, which we found showed significant variations, especially at the poles, with the energy distribution being symmetrical and following a normal distribution, while the particle distributions were asymmetrical and followed a bell curve. We used another method to validate the data and models by comparing the data from the first four close approaches with the data from the second four close approaches, which we found showed consistent results. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates its versatility by effortlessly adapting to new domains within 15 minutes, a substantial reduction from conventional methods that require substantial amounts of time and data. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zhong-jian/sent_adapt. The proposed technique has the potential to enhance the performance of speech-emotion recognition in real-world live data settings with minimal requirements for additional data and time. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. Furthermore, our research successfully reconstructs the time evolution of stress variations from these emissions, demonstrating good agreement with experimental data. The method we have tailored for this analysis is a robust signal processing approach that can be applied to the complex dynamics of real systems, even in situations with intense noise interference. This approach has significant potential, as evidenced by the stress variation time evolution reconstructions, making it a valuable tool for interpreting intricate time-evolution data. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Ultimately, this research provides a concise and precise framework for estimating hedging costs that can be useful for various risk management purposes, including the computation of VaR and the estimation of funding requirements for option portfolios. Furthermore, it lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive examination of the dynamics of hedging costs in response to stock price fluctuations and other market variables. The proposed method can be integrated into existing Monte Carlo simulations, thereby offering a practical solution for addressing the challenges associated with the generation of delta processes in Markovian models. The limitations of the delta-hedging method also are addressed, and the study highlights the potential benefits of using more sophisticated hedging strategies, such as stochastic gamma-hedging. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from the original purpose of optimizing a common objective. To address this issue, we propose a framework based on graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) that enables the optimization of a common objective in the presence of adversaries. Adversarial agents within this framework are assumed to manipulate fake data in their updates. We then pose an optimization problem that accounts for the effects of these malicious actions. To solve this optimization problem, we develop a novel algorithm that uses GCNNs and data cleansing methods. This algorithm is robust in the presence of malicious agents and provides an efficient and secure collaboration mechanism. To validate our approach, we conduct simulations with large scales. Notably, our results show that this approach can effectively reduce the impact of malicious agents when there are thousands of participants. To further illustrate the benefits of our approach, we compare it with a naive approach that involves rejecting all fake data, which leads to an increased burden on collaboration, but with different outcomes. While both approaches result in a reduced impact of malicious agents in small-scale simulations, our approach outperforms the naive approach in large-scale scenarios by a significant margin. This margin continues to grow as the scale increases. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made our code available publicly. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The code is designed to be used in a Markov Chain Monte Carlo framework for an end-to-end analysis of the BICEP/Keck Array experiment. The software is an open source platform that can be modified by the community to adapt it for other similar experiments. The paper also outlines possible future applications of this package, including a discussion of techniques for assessing point process data models and the integration of this package with other cosmic microwave background analysis tools. The's4cmb' package is an openly accessible tool, available at https://github.com/StevenKerr/s4cmb. The associated metadata have been deposited in the Open Science Framework at https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/5e7dca. The firmware and raw data for the TDM bolometer demonstrator can be found in the following repositories: https://github.com/StevenKerr/tmb-demospec-firmware and https://github.com/StevenKerr/tmb-demospec-data, respectively. The FEB-1 firmware is also available at https://github.com/StevenKerr/tmb-demospec-firmware/tree/master/firmware/FEB-1. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. Lastly, we propose a straightforward generation-based approach using BART and evaluate it on the task of ordering unordered words, resulting in improved scores when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Our proposed model attains an exact F-score of 92.1% on the Word Ordering Dataset, surpassing the preceding record by a considerable margin of 3.5%. We also observe positive outcomes using our model on additional datasets including the Natural Language Inference Dataset and the Treebank Dataset although these were achieved with perfect F-scores of 100%. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhuyonghu/word-ordering.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our proposed MD-CSDNetwork achieves remarkable performance, exceeding top models through simpler and more efficient feature extraction, as indicated by reduced parameter counts in models compared to Baseline ResNet-50. Our research hopes to contribute a promising detection method and a usable network architecture for deepfake classification. Our code has been made available on GitHub at: https://github.com/HengtaiZheng/MD-CSDNetwork. Our dataset partition files are available upon request. Our research underscores the significance of exploring domain knowledge and the potential benefits of combined spatial and frequency information in deepfake detection. Our proposed MD-CSDNetwork achieves outstanding performance on existing benchmarks and serves as a viable base models for further incremental learning-based detection methods. Our code and additional information can be found at: https://hengtaizheng.github.io/projects/MD-CSDNetwork/. We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the hypergentiled braid group algebra H_q(B_q). Leveraging the hypergentile structure of the braid group algebra, we find a natural basis for U_q(g) denoted as O_q, consisting of polynomials defined within the ring generated by the hypergentile variables. We then determine the fusion product on the basis O_q, rendering U_q(g) a subalgebra of H_q(B_q) with respect to the star product. Consequently, the quantum group U_q(g) regains its initial structure within the hypergentile framework, allowing us to define its dual representation, thereby obtaining the representation of the quantum group U_q(ˆg) for the complex conjugate Lie algebra ˆg. Ultimately, this enables us to establish a natural representation for the quantum group U_q(ˆg) from a given representation of U_q(g), encompassing both the original and its dual representations. Moreover, we resolve the issue of representability for U_q(ˆg) in the context of the cluster model by broadening the domain of its star-invariant polynomials to include the extended ring generated by the hypergentile variables and their conjugates. Ultimately, this leads to a natural representation for U_q(ˆg) derived from a given representation of U_q(g), thereby establishing an isomorphism between them. We achieve this for the quantum groups U_q(g) corresponding to Lie algebras of type ADE, as well as the exceptional hyperbolic Kac-Moody algebras, by systematically applying the same methodologies established for the finite types. We also explore and resolve various related issues, including the star-invariant polynomials and powers within the hypergentile framework, thereby uncovering new insights into the underlying structure of the quantum groups U_q(g) and the rigid cluster models. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for further advancements in the realm of quantum groups and cluster theories. We also present additional mathematical structures and examples that emerge from the hypergentile framework, including the braid group algebras H_q(B_q), the quantum group U_q(g), the Weyl group invariant subalgebras H_q(B_q)/B_q, the tight hypergentile variables

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our analysis enables us to outline a potential investigative pathway for future research into other, non-transparent pyramid schemes built into blockchain smart contracts. Our Forsage dataset, comprising over 288,000 user transactions, 21,000 code execution logs, and 1,000 promotional videos, is readily available for download or access through an interactive dashboard on our website.
In this research, our key observations regarding the Forsage scheme and its users are as follows: 

- The scheme's blockchain smart contract accurately reflects its advertised, decentralized nature, yet our findings confirm Forsage as a traditional pyramid scheme with a hidden and complex structure. 
- To participate in Forsage, users must purchase Forsage tokens (FSG) from existing members, either immediately losing 90% of their initial investment or facing a 90-day wait to potentially recoup their funds. 
- Our transaction analysis reveals a highly skewed distribution of earnings, with the top 0.1% of participants earning 40% of the total revenue generated by the scheme, indicating significant income inequality among users. 
- To become one of the top earners, users must recruit other members quickly, which we achieved through various means, including social media, online communities, and influencer marketing. 
- Our examination of the scheme's code and transactions shows that Forsage tokens have no utility other than being used to recruit new members, which further supports the classification of Forsage as a traditional pyramid scheme.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. Lastly, a previously unexplored connection between this pentagon code and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition has been established. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is a minimax discourse in the domain of sequence levels. Current approaches train the discriminator on generated sequences, which presents a significant challenge due to the vast number of possible sequences. We argue that a more effective method exists, one that trains the discriminator on a subset of actual sequences, specifically the sequences that the generator fails to produce. We call this method adversarial sequence selection, which provides a potential solution to the difficulties associated with GANs and allows the discriminator to focus on generating critical adversarial examples. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to a text generation model and compare it to standard GAN training. Our results show that adversarial sequence selection significantly improves the quality of the generated text. We also explore various implementations of the method, including a straightforward random selection approach and more sophisticated methods utilizing the discriminator's output, which we found significantly improve the results. Our adversarial sequence selection framework can be applied to various GAN implementations and text generation tasks, and we recommend it as a straightforward and effective method for improving the quality of the generated text. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhw2018/SSGAN. Our results also highlight the potential of adversarial sequence selection in enhancing the performance of large-scale industrial text generation models. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. A global analysis of these clusters reveals a statistical connection between pairs of stars that are closer together, suggesting the possibility that microbial life could be transferred from one star to another, however this result needs further confirmation. Numerical simulations of a protoplanetary disk also reveal the possibility of long-distance transfer of life forms through the scattering of small particles, adding weight to the idea that interstellar panspermia is worthy of further investigation. Overall, a mathematical approach provides a framework for examining the validity of interstellar panspermia, a concept that challenges our current understanding of life's origins. If the phenomenon of interstellar panspermia does exist, it is predicted that most of the evidence will be found in the form of extant life forms rather than the remains of extinct life, and as such, a search for life on exoplanets needs to consider both surface and subsurface environments. The discussion that follows highlights the difficulties of testing interstellar panspermia through observations, but the development of a mathematical model also reveals potential pathways for verifying this idea through the study of local planetary systems, the scattering of small particles, and the migration of stars within clusters. The most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia are found to be pairs of life-bearing planetary systems in open and globular star clusters, which could potentially be the result of microbial life transfer between the two. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  We have made the model and associated R package code available for public use.  This code enables users to employ our method and evaluate the performance of the proposed models through simulation studies.  We further highlight potential applications and extensions of this method in wildlife research. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The robustness of the algorithm is established through a general theorem whose applicability spans various protocol examples, including a decentralized version of the counting algorithm based on degree-hopping, as well as a counting method utilizing a combination of randomFS and Ortega's algorithm known as rF2. The development of rF2 enables the extension of Ortega's algorithm to networks containing a substantial number of malicious nodes. The introductory section of this paper outlines the problem, while the third section presents the algorithm and associated theoretical guarantees, and the fourth section provides a specific protocol example. The fifth section explores various applications of the algorithm, while the sixth section delves into the implementation details and the resulting performance. The seventh section addresses the issue of scalability through a pseudospecific protocol variant known as rF2-light, followed by the conclusion and future work sections. The paper's supplementary material includes additional technical proofs, protocol implementation details, and realistic network simulations. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Moreover, a detailed analysis of solution stability is provided by systematically varying key parameters and comparing the results with existing data. Overall, this method offers a robust, field-independent approach for constructing self-consistent initial data. Given its success in solving the Hamiltonian constraint for rotating black holes with scalar clouds--a scenario known for its solution instability--it is plausible that this method can be used to study such unstable solutions and related phenomena.
