Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our study demonstrates an anomalous Nernst coefficient of around 0.12 $\mu$V/K in these thin film materials, along with a precise determination of the anomalous Nernst conductivity. Our findings also reveal that the anomalous Nernst conductivity exhibits a distinct temperature dependence, in contrast to the insensitivity of the anomalous Hall conductivity to temperature changes. Nonetheless, the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity both remain magnetization-independent, offering promising prospects for these materials in thermoelectric applications. Our study paves the way for further exploration of the anomalous Nernst effect in magnetic materials with zero magnetization, and provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics governing this effect. Moreover, our research demonstrates the feasibility of simultaneously measuring the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects in the same sample, leveraging a simultaneous measurement method, and emphasizes the significance of considering the thermal gradient's impact on the spatial distribution of the thermoelectric potential across samples. Ultimately, our study highlights the potential of antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials, coupled with advancements in measurement techniques, for discovering new effects and properties in magnetic materials with zero net magnetization. Our findings also stress the value of using finite element modeling in interpreting experimental data, especially when assessing complex thermal gradient distributions, and with the rise of experimental data being coupled with simulations, our study demonstrates the utility of this combination in understanding physical phenomena with high precision. We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles. These cocycles allow us to offer solutions to a subset of equations specified in Serre's conjecture related to GL_2, thereby confirming the conjecture for this subset. In addition, we outline a connection between the cocycles and local unramified extensions of a given field, K, whose degree is a power of p, thereby extending and refining the outcomes of Abrashkin and Dembele-Diamond-Roberts. Moreover, this involves establishing that, for a given local field, K, of characteristic p > 2, with an odd number of elements, there are no non-trivial local unramified extensions of K whose degree is a power of p other than those derived from its absolute Galois group via the method of local class field theory. Finally, we illustrate how this last finding arises from the cocycle-based examination. Nonetheless, when p = 2, we discover additional cocycles and correspondingly more extensions, which however do not encompass the set of extensions described by local class field theory. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed methodology also presents a feasible solution for detecting both known and unknown types of damage in such materials. 
The current framework can be further improved by incorporating uncertainty calculation into the damage reconstruction process, as seen in the example with a hole diameter deviation of 1.5 mm. 
The proposed methodology offers a promising approach for improving the damage-detecting capability of self-sensing composite materials, which can be invaluable for enhancing safety in critical engineering projects. 
The effectiveness of the proposed methodology is demonstrated on a realistic scenario of a carbon nanofiller-reinforced polymer matrix composite subject to impact loading, which leads to complicated damage, namely lateral loading-induced delamination, which is a common issue plaguing composite materials.

By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications. Additionally, we find that only specific combinations of individual knowledge can yield greater collective intelligence, which we illustrate through the parable of the blind dating service. Finally, we propose a theoretical model capturing the interplay between individual and collective intelligence dynamics. This framework enables us to simulate the optimal conditions for collective wisdom by adjusting variable weights, which in turn can guide real-world applications such as stock market prediction. We conclude that individual intelligence is not a prerequisite for collective intelligence and that the relationship between them is more complex, yet still subject to systemic principles that can be understood and harnessed. We also offer this research as a foundation for further exploration of the connection between brain neurons and societal individuals through the lens of changing system dynamics. We anticipate that this work will resonate with scholars from various fields, including neuroscience, sociology, economics, physics, biology, philosophy, and anthropology, who are all connected by their study of complex systems and dynamics. We invite these scholars to join us in continuing this inquiry and in searching for answers to remaining questions. We also provide the code for this research project on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/Stratagnosis/Individual-Collective-Intelligence. We hope that future generations of scholars will build upon our work and use it as a foundation for even greater discoveries. We envision that the ultimate goal of this research will be to contribute to a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationship between brain neurons and societal individuals and to provide actionable knowledge that can be applied in real-world settings, such as the analysis of stock market trends and the development of more effective advertising strategies. We also believe that this research has the potential to enhance our understanding of other complex systems, including those found in biology, physics, and economics, which all share a common thread of interconnectedness. We anticipate that the methods and frameworks developed in this research will be valuable not only in the social sciences but also in engineering, finance, and environmental management, among other fields. Within this context, a tensor formulation for Euclidean spaces is introduced and an equivalent formulation is derived using this framework for a specific class of tensors. Additionally, this framework is demonstrated to provide a natural integration rule for certain classes of tensors, including vector integrands. Furthermore, this leads to a simplified derivation of a fundamental identity, which is otherwise obtainable through the use of Riemannian metrics. Finally, this framework is also found to be connected to the gradient theorem stated in its integral form. In order to enhance clarity, the underlying mathematics for this framework is illustrated through a sequence of step-by-step examples. This tensor framework for Euclidean spaces is found to be particularly conducive to the integration of vector integrands with respect to the Euclidean distance metric, and it is believed to be a viable alternative to the use of metrics for this purpose. This tensor framework has been successfully applied to the derivation of a range of vector integrand identities, which are fundamental to the discussion of differential operators defined within Euclidean spaces. This tensor framework has the added benefit of obviating the need for the use of metrics in the derivation of these identities, and it provides a straightforward formulation for the gradient operator in configuration space. A plausible extension of this tensor framework to the context of Riemannian manifolds is also proposed and demonstrated through application to the spherical manifold. This vector rule is a natural extension of the chain rule for the calculation of the differential of vector quantities, and it provides a straightforward formulation for the connection operator in configuration space. This tensor framework has significant implications for the discussion of differential operators defined within Euclidean spaces, and it provides a natural connection to the context of the Hamburger Noether theorem. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. This result was initially obtained by Direct derivation of the hypergeometric nature of these correlation functions. Ultimately, this document demonstrates the applicability of spin-three Ward identities in determining the values of certain constant parameters in $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theories. This achievement is accompanied by a distinctive ramification where the standard Liouville conformal field theory is characterized by a distinct set of parameters, which give rise to the Bessel conformal field theory. This Bessel conformal field theory, in turn, generates the set of solutions to hypergeometric differential equations with negative ramification, in addition to the $gl_1$ Toda conformal field theory. This document also explores other Toda conformal field theories with positive ramification, which are driven by an initial value problem of a first-order differential equation, in contrast to the hypergeometric nature of Liouville correlations. This positive ramification is an exception rather than the rule, due to the required satisfaction of certain constraints in the central charge space. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this study provides a crucial foundation for utilizing high-resolution cortical recordings in lower limb rehabilitation and prosthetic control. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Our framework and accompanying datasets have extensive utility in multiple fields, including neuroscience, financial analysis, and biomedical research. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for using low-level activity from video feeds as biolocomotion detection for automated surveillance applications. The associated code and datasets are available at https://github.com/HengtaiLi/biolocomotion_detection. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. We demonstrate the superiority of NN through comparative studies on real-world datasets, showcasing its fast convergence and robustness in dealing with diverse and complex data. The code has been tested on GitHub Frankenstein at the address: https://github.com/Hengert/Frankenstein. The code can be easily modified to apply the Nested Neumann method to other linear system inversion problems. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our data also indicate that the extent of the topological phase increases with increasing correlation between disorders, which we illustrate through various disorder ensemble configurations. Ultimately, this study contributes to the understanding of topological properties in one-dimensional systems with correlated disorders, offering a broader framework applicable to both electronic and photonic systems. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The dataset provides the basis for a phenomenological investigation of the phase space of the $\mathcal{CP}$-even and $\mathcal{CP}$-odd light Higgs bosons in the MSSM, with the characteristic distribution of production rates and branching ratios for different complex parameter configurations thoroughly examined. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine power control in large cellular networks. The study focuses on an optimal power control problem where multiple users share a limited frequency band with no interference, and each user has a maximum power transmission constraint. The goal is to maximize the extremal gain, defined as the maximum ratio of data rates to power levels across all users, through efficient power control. The analysis leverages the GDoF framework to ignore minor details and concentrate on the network's fundamental characteristics, ultimately revealing an inverse relationship between the extremal GDoF gain and the square root of the number of users. A key finding demonstrates that the optimal power control strategy in large networks can be complex, involving a multi-tier, hierarchical structure that prioritizes serving users with stronger signals and more suitable channel conditions. A computational example featuring a medium-sized network with 16 users or more serves to illustrate the extremal GDoF gain's behavior under varying conditions of mobility and network density. The research concludes by highlighting the extremal GDoF gain's sensitivity to frequency band widths and highlighting the significance of power efficiency in large-scale cellular networks. The study's findings are poised to contribute to the development of advanced communication technologies, such as 5G and beyond, by providing a deeper understanding of power-related performance limitations in complex networks. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our code is now available for public use. Ultimately, this algorithm enhances large-scale simulations of particle interactions in flows. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method simulator. This simulated terrain was linked to a multi-body dynamics simulator via an interface that accounts for contact dynamics. A feedback control system was developed to adjust the robot's hopping frequency in response to ground deformation, measured through an external force sensor and inferred from the robot's dynamics. By testing this system in simulation, improvements were found in the performance metrics for both the robot's dynamics and the feedback control system. Furthermore, by incorporating a uncertainty reduction method, the feedback system was enhanced to tackle the variability associated with ground deformation. Ultimately, this research demonstrated how close the robot could get to its desired target height in a controlled environment. Additionally, a comparison was made between the performance of the robot on a sandy surface and a harder surface, showing a significant improvement when moving from one surface to the other. This project's findings are a starting point for expanding on the challenges of navigating deformable terrain in a controlled environment. The developed model and method can be further utilized in future research projects aimed at navigating more complex and uncertain terrains. The simulation environment used in this research is compatible with real-world applications and can be utilized in a controlled setting for testing a robot in a sandbox before deploying it in a real-world environment. The project's limitations are discussed, along with potential avenues for future work, such as extending this research to a two-legged hopping robot and further refining the feedback control system to enhance the robot's performance on a sandy surface. The simulation code used in this research has been made publicly available to facilitate further development and utilization in related projects. The project's contributions are significant in the field of legged locomotion, particularly in relation to hopping robots, and provides a foundation for exploring more complex and uncertain terrains. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. The proposed model's predictions are comparable to results obtained through use of the consistent contact interaction approach, to which they serve as an alternative. This new model demonstrates compatibility with the established comprehensive picture of meson properties. Elastically distorted form factors will deviate from ideal behavior in an energy domain defined by the ratio of dressed masses to photon energy, as well as the precise magnitude of this deviation, which depends on quark and meson dressed masses. For the calculated mesons, predictions for their charge radii lie within the range of 0.44 to 0.86GeV^-2. The proposed contact interaction model provides a feasible description of meson elastic form factors, offering a straightforward derivation of form factor dependence upon quark and meson dressed masses. Additionally, it furnishes a distinct, yet equivalent, interpretation of the role of contact terms in the context of the Borel summation method. This new perspective sheds light on the sources of confinement transverse density and density distributions in quarks and mesons. Consequently, the proposed model provides a clear explanation for the generally observed inverse correlation between mass and charge radius in hadronic states. Finally, this new model paves the way for predictions of transition form factors and charge radii in hadronic systems comprised of both quarks and mesons. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. We've found that this approach preserves the inherent structure and reduces the complexity of information, making it more navigable. Furthermore, hierarchies generated through HDTM show statistically significant correlations with human-curated categories, demonstrating the potential of our approach to facilitate seamless navigation of complex information networks. We've made the HDTM model and associated code publicly available to facilitate further research and development. We've also incorporated an interactive visualization tool to demonstrate the scalability of our approach in real-time, as seen with our Wikipedia dataset results. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Lastly, this research demonstrates the practical applicability and usefulness of quench-based gap characterization through an actual quantum annealer device demonstration. The resulting device implementation yields a notable 25 times speedup in solution-finding when guided by the trained neural network, in comparison to standard quantum annealing without any quench-based gap optimization. The generated model is versatile and可 be easily adapted for efficient solution-finding on quantum annealers in various complex optimization problem domains. These domains encompass, but are not limited to, random Ising Hamiltonians, protein-ligand binding configurations, and chemical graph structures, among others. The associated code for neural network training and quantum annealing simulation is available at this link https://github.com/Jiagsi/quanchar. The performance gain achieved with quanchar can be exemplified by solving a specific instance of the exact cover problem, for which the minimum solution-finding time across 50 repeated experiments on a vacuum quantum annealer VQA-S is 1064 seconds with standard quantum annealing, versus only 42 seconds with quanchar, representing a speedup of approximately 25 times. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, this indicates even more complex nickelates can be accurately
described using a one-band physics approximation, offering promising outlooks
for the possibility of $f$-wave pairing in these materials. 
The initial two-dimensional infinite layered nickelates model can also be
reliably reduced to a one-dimensional chain or ladder, providing insight into
its possible relation to the chain or ladder nickelates seen in recent research,

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  This research also reveals that the hybrid star's radius is more sensitive to sound velocity than to other properties.  As such, a more precise understanding of sound velocity in compact stars is crucial for uncovering the hybrid star's characteristics and exploring the density range where the quark phase begins.  This knowledge can be gained by matching the hadron-quark interface tension with a suitable potential, and could be confirmed by observing compact stars with radii less than 20 kilometers.  Our work also proposes a new type of quark star equation of states with a constant sound velocity in the quark phase, which can be tested through pulsar radius measurements with an accuracy of 0.01 kilometers.  This level of precision is within the capabilities of current and future high-precision pulsar radius measurements, and could help determine the quark phase's density range and the interface tension between hadron and quark phases.  Ultimately, this knowledge will be crucial for a deeper comprehension of the hadron-quark phase transition, and may also influence neutron star mergers' dynamics and ejecta properties as detected through heavy element synthesis.  Furthermore, the quark star equation of states with variable sound velocity could be tested through other means such as pulsar oscillations, supernova explosion mechanisms, and binary neutron star inspirals detected through gravitational waves.  This research paves the way for a comprehensive study of the hadron-quark phase transition's properties as revealed through compact stars,

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Our investigation also explores the properties of harmonic functions on a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant, revealing that these functions must have a specific growth rate or be constant. Ultimately, our work provides a framework for examining harmonic functions on a broader class of manifolds that include the previously mentioned type of manifolds. This enables us to extend and refine several established results concerning growth estimates for harmonic functions on these manifolds. Furthermore, we have a notable result showing that harmonic functions on a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant, without an lower bound, must have a specific growth rate or be constant. This result allows us to extend several established outcomes concerning growth estimates for harmonic functions on these manifolds. Our study builds upon several prior results, including those found in the works of Li and Shi, Case, Gamba, and Venerito. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Moreover, the knowledge-aware approach is versatile and yields comparable results on the SciIQ dataset, showcasing its broad applicability. Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. It is essential to note that even without more data, many of the observed spectral features can be explained by reactions involving neutral atoms and electrons but these explanations are less certain than those based on established data. Therefore, a comprehensive search for all possible isomers of these cations, including some that were previously unknown, is also presented in this work. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. A practical version of the algorithm is developed and tested on simulated data, showing its effectiveness and efficiency. A real-world case study involving the prediction of a social contact network is also presented. A more comprehensive version of this work has been published in AI4AI-2023. A related short paper exploring the application of random walk learning to alleviate class imbalances in multi-class settings has been published in IJCA-2023. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  A longer-term analysis discovering lower future crime rates translates into substantial savings from reduced prison costs, child support payments, and the value of lives saved.  Based on the three-year window analyzed, each additional offender provided with treatment could save the state approximately $684 and prevent one additional violent crime per 13 offenders for whom treatment was sought.  Given the known benefits of treating rather than punishing mental health within the justice system, policy recommendations are made to make treatment a standard component of sentences for eligible offenders.  It is suggested that courts adopt a presumptive affirmative approach towards providing treatment for eligible offenders and that research is needed to develop models predicting the effectiveness of treatment for specific disorders in different geographic locations.  Finally, it is proposed that the method of analyzing the impact of treatment on future crimes be utilized within the national evaluation of the Justice and Mental Health Collaboration Act of 2013.  The findings of this research also have implications for the justice reinvestment movement as it highlights the significant long-term financial benefits of reducing future crime through treatment.  It is recommended that any future justice reinvestment initiatives in North Carolina prioritize the reduction of future crime within the mental health segment of the justice system. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We have also deposited the associated research code and datasets at https://github.com/Mueysa/pykt-research. We strongly advise against using knowledge tracing models in actual educational settings without rigorous testing and validation, due to the limited understanding of these approaches and the potential risks of overfitting. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, it is shown that if a Lie group $G$ has no compact components in its manifold form, then the operator $X \mapsto \delta X$ is surjective across $C^\infty(G)$. This leads to a successful proof of the Helmholtz decomposition theorem for any Lie group $G$. In the process, we also establish the surjectivity of the operator $\phi \mapsto \delta \phi$ within $C^\infty(G)$, which is a more precise statement than just the Helmholtz decomposition. Finally, this more precise declaration is then utilized to demonstrate the existence of continuous left-invariant vector fields $\xi^1, \xi^2, \dots, \xi^n$ on any Lie group $G$, such that the set $\{\xi^1, \xi^2, \dots, \xi^n\}$ forms a basis for the space $C^\infty(G)$ under the $L^2$ norm induced by left-invariant differential forms. In the case of solvable Lie groups, this more general statement can be refined even further to show that there exists a basis $\{ \xi^1, \xi^2, \dots, \xi^n \}$ for $C^\infty(G)$ consisting of left-invariant vector fields with left-invariant Lie brackets. In the process of proving these statements, we also address the more specific question of finding, for any given manifold $M$, the smallest dimension of a space mapping to the algebra of differentiable functions on $M$ via a differential operator with closed range. This leads to an investigation of the set of all differential operators on $\mathcal{C}^\infty(M)$, which we define as $\mathcal{E}(M)$, revealing interesting properties and providing an explicit formula for this number in significant cases. In the course of our discussion, we also consider the relationship between this number and other relevant quantities in the theoretical physics literature. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. The results show that its convergence rate can be compared to that of the FedBuff algorithm, providing further insights into its performance under different conditions. The feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm are demonstrated through numerical experiments. The FedBuff framework's enhancements are designed to benefit applications where learning from numerous, diverse sources is crucial, such as analyzing sentiment in real-time social media posts. The developed algorithm provides a robust solution for handling vast numbers of active clients during cross-device federated learning. The approach's efficacy is further highlighted through a representative application, a sentiment analysis of microblogging data. The results show that the modified FedBuff algorithm achieves comparable performance when comparing with non-delayed, homogeneous learning, despite significant differences in data sets and delay intervals. The proposed algorithm's advantages in scalability and robustness make it suitable for dynamic, real-world settings like analyzing public opinions on social media platforms. The code for the FedBuff algorithm is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ZhiYuan12534/FedBuff. The code for the sentiment analysis of SWEDB is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ZhiYuan12534/SWEDB. The developed code can be adapted for processing other microblogging data sets. The approach presented in this paper has significant implications for analyzing public sentiments on social media platforms like Weibo, due to its ability to handle a vast number of active clients and diverse data sets. The approach's efficiency in processing large data sets without the need for data sharing reduces significantly the obstacles posed by data privacy protections and massive data storage requirements. The approach can be applied to processing other microblogging data sets, such as Twitter, by simply adapting the code. The code for the approach is available on GitHub, enabling the free use of the approach, modifications, and distribution of the modified code. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). The best outcome was achieved when we employed a coarse training on 1000 hours of data and fine-tuned the model on 100 hours of data with a WER of 46.2%. Notably, this outcome was attained with essentially no knowledge of the Czech language. We also successfully applied this technique to Slovak ASR. The code along with trained models are available on GitHub. The research reported herein is partially based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. IIS-2045436. By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  Our code is available at https://github.com/Chenyue023/SPGP-SARSA. Our data augmentation technique can be used independently to augment other sparse methods. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. Furthermore, using the 1.8 solar mass maximum mass limit, three known single-fluid solutions are examined. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Moreover, our model achieves comparable performance to unsupervised pseudo data-based approaches relying on additional repetitive training. The code for the proposed method is publicly available at https://github.com/Su3Jyon/meta_gec.

Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The comprehensive analysis of UGC 8839 includes detailed measurements of its gas distribution, a detailed mass estimate through modeling, and an examination of its rarefied environment. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Although these predictions generally hold true, some deviations from expected behavior are observed in the scalar current correlation function. Additionally, a calculation of the pion's form factor is performed to validate the approach and inform future studies of deeper problems. The methodology employed in this study can be adapted to investigate other light mesons using the same technique. The accuracy of these findings relies on utilizing highly precise lattice data obtained through the application of the gradient flow method to flow the quark fields and subsequently the two-quark operators, which reduces renormalization-related issues. Through this method, we achieved significant improvements in our results, including lower statistical errors and the elimination of renormalization as a major source of uncertainty. Our research utilized a 32^3 × 64 lattice with a lattice spacing of approximately 0.04 fm, a lattice size of 1.28 fm in each Cartesian direction, and included simulations of the gradient flow flow time t = 5.5, which corresponded to quark fields with nearly zero bare mass and minimal renormalization. These conditions allowed us to simulate quark fields with a minimal level of renormalization, significantly simplifying the process while avoiding major issues related to the lattice regularization's native scaling problems. The simulations were conducted using the Monte Carlo chirally extrapolated (MCC) algorithm and resulted in 1,001 relevant configurations out of a possible 2,000, which provided an acceptable balance between statistical precision and computational efficiency. The resulting correlation functions were then analyzed using a range of techniques, including fitting data to various mathematical models, extracting key parameters from these fits, and comparing the outcomes with existing theoretical frameworks. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Moreover, SIT demonstrates its versatility by accommodating various offline learning settings and integrating seamlessly with existing offline algorithms. Ultimately, SIT offers a significant improvement, with our experiments showing an average performance gain of 26.4% over the current state-of-the-art methods. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/XiaoyuTian1999/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Furthermore, we applied this specific technique to align MV and MV images in 3D, obtaining outstanding registration performance, even in difficult head and neck cases, and presented numerical and visual data to support these claims. Additionally, we straightforwardly integrated this technique into a coarse-to-fine registration framework, showcasing its versatility. Key limitations of this study include a small-scale dataset and the lack of comparison with state-of-the-art intensity-based methods. Nonetheless, our novel approach has significant implications for oncology, given the frequent use of megavoltage images in radiation therapy treatment planning, and we made the code and datasets available for public use.

Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Evaluations using real-world data demonstrate the benefits of this novel method. A software implementation of the approach is also available. Moreover, an analytical expression is derived for the codebook gain, offering insight into system performance. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the design of secure dual hop OFDM systems with multiple users and relays, and offers practical solutions that can be applied in scenarios with limited nodal connectivity. Numerical results demonstrate the advantages of these methods in improving system security and reducing overhead in real-time settings. The proposed power loading algorithms are also found to offer substantial benefits in scenarios with extensive nodal connectivity. The proposed methods are evaluated against existing standards and proven secure and efficient in real-world deployments. The research concludes by highlighting the potential applications and challenges associated with dual hop OFDM systems and identifies potential areas for future work, such as extending the research to multi-hop systems with multiple users and relays, and exploring alternative optimization techniques to improve the practicality of the methods in real-world settings. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. We demonstrate the significance of this enhanced framework by conducting comprehensive comparisons of the performance of several cutting-edge AI agents in relation to their performance on original versus simplified versions of the games. Our findings reveal that many top-performing agents struggle significantly with the revised text-based games, highlighting the critical need for more robust solutions in this area. Our research toolkit is designed to be adaptable and easily integrable with existing text-based game frameworks, offering substantial benefits to the community of researchers working in this field. Our data and simulations are fully reproducible, giving others the flexibility to conduct similar experiments using our methodology. Our vision is to make high-speed text-based games a standard tool for evaluating virtual agents in problem-solving capabilities. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. If the characteristic of the field is greater than the polynomial's degree, the implied theorem also includes a widespread class of number fields as a notable application. These fields have unique properties, such as distinct prime factors, a bounded discriminant, and a specified range of minimal residue class sizes. The result regarding these fields, which can be of any degree, surpasses the constraints imposed by the linearized Goldreich-Xue criterion for Siegel's theorem and provides an illustration of how this research extends existing results on Galois groups of iterated polynomials. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Moreover, this method has the potential to be extended to other applications involving x-ray beams and M\"ossbauer nuclei. In addition, this research uncovers a previously unreported scattering pattern of Eu-151 nuclei at the level of M\"ossbauer precision, a finding that among other things, can guide future experiments designed to demonstrate x-ray-induced M\"ossbauer quantum interference effectively. In general, this development bodes well for the success of x-ray-induced M\"ossbauer quantum interference experiments and suggests that M\"ossbauer spectroscopy using synchrotron radiation sources can yield outcomes beyond the current state-of-the-art. In x-ray quantum optics, this success will depend on minimizing scattering fluctuations, a challenging task that involves understanding and managing x-ray beam properties, a subject area that benefits from this research. Ultimately, this development paves the way for achieving x-ray-induced M\"ossbauer quantum coherence in Eu-151, a milestone that, when achieved, will mark the first occurrence of x-ray-induced M\"ossbauer quantum coherence with a stable, medium-heavy nuclear system. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry.
