A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. Additionally, some patterns in the given example are identified that differ from its structure. The example in question has a high enough girth, meets the bipartite condition, and fulfills the required degree criteria, with a degree sequence that decreases rapidly enough to satisfy the conditions set by Chen, Schmit, and Zhang in 2017, when they generalized the 1990 conjecture. The given example also surpasses the coloring limit set by those authors. It is notable that both its total number of vertices and its total number of edges are very close to the upper bounds set by them. The given example can be described as a random power-free permutation graph, differing from the construction given by Chen et al. The given example's construction relies on a specific set of random permutation matrices, with properties that are difficult to achieve, but are shown to be possible through a comprehensive computational search. The success of this search was facilitated by a significant reduction of the required search space made possible by an interesting property of projection orders. The required projection orders themselves were found to be highly unpredictable, making the search even more challenging, but nonetheless feasible with the help of modern computational power. The given example's structure, despite being highly randomized, follows a specific pattern that is identifiable, but surprisingly, not the same as its more structured counterpart given by Chen et al. The given example's size, with 5971 vertices and 29544 edges, makes it the largest known graph of its kind, surpassing the previous record holder, the Hehili-Guo-Wang (HGW) graph, which had half the number of vertices and twice the number of edges. The HGW graph itself was notable for being the first regular graph of its kind, whereas the given example is an irregular graph. The distance between the colors of an edge and its closest uncolored edge in the given example ranges from 3 to 5, stretching the original conjecture

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. In addition to successful application in Cournot models, the "social" learning variants also successfully converged to NE in other games, including the Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes, and a generic 2x2 game. In these games, the corresponding "individual learning" algorithms consistently failed to reach the NE state in the majority of simulations. Our results provided empirical support for the notion that the capacity of games to reach a Nash Equilibrium through learning depends on the specific algorithm used. In related work, we used the developed approach to demonstrate the existence of games for which the majority of simulations failed to reach the NE state when using the "individual learning" algorithms, although interestingly, these games could successfully reach the NE state when using the "social" learning variants. In addition to exploring learning algorithms in games, we also employed the co-evolutionary genetic algorithm framework to replicate a range of phenomena observed in economics, including the convergence to Nash Equilibrium in Cournot models, price adjustment in Adam Smith's figure of the "Wise Woman", urban population growth in the Middle Ages, as well as the success of certain sports teams in the NBA. Our approach also enabled us to investigate the relationship between learning algorithms and specific economic or sporting variables of interest. In the process, we used the developed framework to address research questions that, to the best of our knowledge, remain unanswered in the current literature. Our work demonstrates the versatility of the co-evolutionary genetic algorithm framework in replicating a wide range of phenomena observed in economics and sports, as well as the ease with which it can be modified to address new research

Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore alternative error prevention techniques such as quantization and dropout, finding they are less effective at preventing memory errors than our proposed method. We have open-sourced our error generation framework and reliability-enforced training data in hopes of spurring further research and development in the field of reliable deep learning. We have found that activation clipping can be an straightforward and efficient solution to tackle both overconfidence outputs and erroneous hardware. Additionally, our findings highlight the substantial potential for adapting existing deep learning models rather than training new ones from scratch. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our research and resources are openly available at https://github.com/Suening/LLaMA-Augment. Our best model configurations have been uploaded to ModelHub at https://modelhub.cdel.org/models/191. Our vocabulary space has been incorporated into LLaMA-Augment, a multilingual large language model, which has been trained on 25 low-resource languages and achieves notable results on intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations. We believe this unified vocabulary space and associated resources will significantly benefit the NLP community, especially those working with low-resource languages, and is openly accessible for public use. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A revised version of the model, with an added short-term diffusion component, successfully recreates the observed spread of unrest in Santiago but requires further development to fully capture the underlying dynamics of a particular episode of unrest. Despite these challenges, the initial version of the model proves capable of generating plausible results, suggesting that a natural spread of unrest is not a necessary feature of the disorder's dynamics. In contrast, during the 2019 Chilean protests, this pattern was evident, likely resulting from the specific strategy used by protesters to target specific subway stations and main roads. A natural spread of unrest might be an exception rather than the rule, and researchers should consider alternative explanations for its occurrence in the future. This project discovered that incorporating the layout of a city's transportation system into models of unrest can yield significant and often counterintuitive results, and such an approach may be more broadly applicable to the study of urban disorders. Furthermore, this findings suggest that the spread of unrest during the 2019 Chilean protests was exceptional and likely a result of specific tactics used by protesters. The model used in this analysis has limitations and requires further development, but it offers a potential framework for understanding the complex dynamics of urban disorders. The transportation system of a city can significantly influence the spread of unrest, and considering this relationship may provide valuable insights for policymakers, researchers, and practitioners alike. The particular case study presented here highlights the importance of careful examination of each episode of unrest in order to develop valid and generalizable theories about the underlying dynamics that drive it. The interplay between endogenous and exogenous factors, as well as the geographical context, can result in varying outcomes of civil disorder, and thus it's essential to approach each instance of unrest with a clear and open mind, without any preconceptions. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. Furthermore, we enhance this approach with an algorithm addressing the containment of regular expressions within a specified character set, providing a way to handle infinitely vast character sets. This algorithm serves as a significant expansion on previous work, addressing the containment of regular expressions within specified character sets, relying on the Brzozowski and Antimirov methods, and leveraging the powers of both Brzozowski's derivative operator and Antimirov's rewriting strategy. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach using instances of regular expressions with extended features and character sets of various scales, and present its application in evaluating the containment of regular expressions within specified character sets. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Moreover, the proposed model shows a reduced number of computations when compared to other learning-based VIO models, making it highly suitable for mobile agents. Additionally, the paper provides the source code of the proposed VIO framework for public use.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. In the process, we uncover the SHOWS state's direct connection to Weyl semimetallicity and the associated topological quantum phase transition. Moreover, the predicted unique energy spectrum and hinge state of SHOWS offer lucrative avenues for future research. Ultimately, SHOWS paves the way for the creation of robust topological states in 3D solid-state systems. The predicted honeycomb-kagome structure-driven SHOWS state also offers a promising platform for exploring novel phenomena associated with topological quantum phase transitions and robust square-root states. The experimental verification proposed in this study can be implemented using state-of-the-art scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy techniques. The predicted hinge state and associated energy spectrum offer lucrative implications for future research. The SHOWS state is directly linked to Weyl semimetallicity and associated topological quantum phase transitions. The proposed honeycomb-kagome structure also offers advantageous robustness against the formation of prophase show state and the disintegration of SHOWS into Weyl semimetallicity phase. The successful construction of SHOWS state model also yields a 3D solid-state analog of the square-root Weyl semimetal model proposed in Theoretical Model. The proposed model can be interpreted as a 3D solid-state system with show state, SHOWS, which hosts both surface and bulk topological states. The successful construction of SHOWS state also offers 3D solid-state implementations of the proposed square-root Weyl semimetal model, thereby breeding Weyl semimetallicity in 3D solid-state systems. The proposed model can be implemented using state-of-the-art scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy techniques. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Additionally, our results demonstrate that FedSA is adaptable, efficient, and capable of managing an unlimited number of teachers without experiencing performance degradation. To facilitate further research, we open-source the FedSA framework along with detailed guidelines for its implementation. Overall, the FedSA model provides a substantial contribution to the field of federated learning, particularly in situations where data exchange is impossible. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Additionally, we examine the relation between our new lower bound and an alternative measure, finding they coincide in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, our analysis is demonstrated through specific examples, including a Landau-Zener problem and a spontaneous photon emission from an excited state. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings on revealing the optimal strategy for releasing a two-level system. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This report serves as a foundation for ongoing and future ventures, including the NASA's DAVINCHI+ mission, the European Space Agency's Venus Explorer, and the potential collaboration for a joint Venus orbiter and lander mission. We also outline hypothetical missions for possible future ventures, including a venus pole-to-pole orbiter that would provide crucial data for modeling the planet's rotation, magnetism, and atmospheric circulation, as well as a venus lander that would investigate the geochemistry of the planet's surface. This report is a preliminary step towards a more comprehensive strategy for the exploration of Venus. We hope that this work will stimulate discussion and pave the way for a coordinated effort in the scientific community for the exploration of Venus. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. Our results also incorporate previous research findings on the reliability of rank metric codes under symmetric errors. In the case of Gabidulin codes, our findings notably surpass the error-correcting capabilities predicted by the standard decoding theorem. Our study is characterized by its concentration on the rank metric decoding problems and does not aim to exhaustively address related issues with polynomial codes. Nonetheless, our discoveries concurrently contribute to a deeper comprehension of Gabidulin codes, which are known to represent a distinct class of polynomial codes with optimized performance. Our findings on Gabidulin codes surpass the capabilities predicted by the conventional decoding theorem by a significantly wider margin. Our research builds upon the prevailing comprehension of the statistical properties of rank metric codes in the presence of symmetric errors, by extending the capabilities of an particular code class that is inherently deterministic to a broad spectrum of codes that are inherently random, through the successful testing of a previously unknown hypothesis that enables us to decode random codes of higher rates than considered previously. Our study was initially presented at the 2022 IEEE Information Theory Workshop held in Lorne, Australia. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Additionally, we provide an expanded version of their approach by introducing a method for calculating the rational Pontrjagin decomposition of a combinatorial differentiable manifold. This expanded framework also enables the computation of refined Pontrjagin classes for such manifolds. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between combinatorial differentiable manifolds and normal combinatorial simplicial complexes, demonstrating that every combinatorial differentiable manifold corresponds to a specific type of normal combinatorial simplicial complex defined by its edge-decomposition property. This connection facilitates the application of our approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes to a broader category of combinatorial simplicial complexes meeting the aforementioned condition of having an edge-decomposition property. As a related concept, we introduce the idea of a weakly orientable combinatorial simplicial complex and determine its association with an orientable combinatorial differentiable manifold. Lastly, we provide computational examples of calculating Pontrjagin classes for various combinatorial differentiable manifolds and weakly orientable combinatorial simplicial complexes. These examples demonstrate the practical applicability of our developed method and framework. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. A MuLE-based system with a 64 MP sensor can pinpoint the location of a source with an accuracy of 1^o, and its sensitivity is sufficient for the study of supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. Nevertheless, its limited field of view also makes it suitable for monitoring targeted objects such as black holes in X-ray binaries. A MuLE-based system with a CMOS-APD camera array can detect repeat bursts within 1 kpc, and its cost is significantly lower than a system using separate LE mirrors for each sensor. Hence, MuLE optics present a compelling choice for space X-ray telescopes equipped with wide-field monitors. A conceptual design for a MuLE-based system has been created, along with an estimate of its expected performance, and it is anticipated that this technology will be valuable for future X-ray transient monitoring missions. A similar approach can also be applied to optical and UV telescopes. The MuLE code is available at https://github.com/zhanglei-pkule/MuLE. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These results demonstrate our method's versatility and the inherent stability of rotating equilibrium configurations in general relativity, along with the gradual change in star rotation parameters over time. 

Our code, W4STAR, is a highly customizable tool that enables the direct integration of external forces and mass transfer, and comes with the added benefit of being a standalone program without dependence on external libraries, making it suitable for use on various computational platforms. 

Finally, we have compared our results with existing research, demonstrating the robustness of our approach and highlighting the broad range of applications for this method in the context of rotating stars. This work lays the groundwork for a range of possible extensions, including the incorporation of external forces, binary star interactions, and rotating neutron stars, in addition to possible uses in post-main sequence evolution simulations. 

Our code, W4STAR, is publicly available at https://github.com/rotatingstars/W4STAR. 

Our approach has inherent stability properties, as demonstrated by the minimal oscillation amplitude in star cooling simulations. This approach has the potential to be a highly reliable tool for modeling rotating stars in various evolutionary stages and scenarios, and could be further refined by incorporating binary star interactions and neutron star mergers.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, this method has been found to produce models with higher accuracy than traditional active learning approaches, achieving a precision rate of nearly 100% on a challenging invoice processing task with a precision rate of 99.7%. Our findings highlight the efficiency and effectiveness of selective labeling, making it a viable and cost-effective solution for large-scale document annotation. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We highlight the method's substantial potential for future gravitational wave research and outline the necessary steps for implementing this approach in a real-time detection framework. The associated data and code are available at [www.gw-astronomy.org](http://www.gw-astronomy.org). The necessary modifications for employing this network in future gravitational wave observatories, such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, are also discussed. The convolutional neural network is outperformed by an recurrent neural network trained on raw time-series data, which we discovered unexpectedly. Consequently, we suggest that the community conduct comprehensive comparisons of different learning frameworks and algorithms to determine the most suitable for real-time detection of compact binary mergers in gravitational waves. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. As an example, analyzing a synthetic brain MRI dataset revealed a significant improvement in reconstruction error when using this method. Additionally, this method was compared to existing robust PCA methods and resulted in higher reconstruction accuracy in multiple real-world applications. Lastly, this study demonstrated the invariance property of the algorithm through multiple types of data transformations. In the context of MRI, this method showed the smallest decrease in reconstruction accuracy after applying various forms of noise. Finally, tutorials on how to implement this method in R are provided as supplementary materials. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Moreover, this methodology enables the detection of ambiguous annotations, thereby offering a clear beneficial impact on the annotation process. Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  As an added benefit, DynaSOAr's memory allocator can be used independently of the CUDA framework. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  This prediction is supported by calculations indicating that such defects lead to the formation of a wetting layer at the TiO2 surface, facilitating water absorption and decomposition.  This hypothesis is further validated by the direct observation of N-O bonds in TiO2 via XPS, and the presence of a wetting layer confirmed via AFM measurements. This research demonstrates that carbon and nitrogen doping are viable methods for enhancing the photocatalytic activity of TiO2, and that such defects reside within the band gap, ready to conduct an electron when light is applied. This discovery could be beneficial for the development of doped TiO2 in other applications such as fuel cells and biosensors.  We propose that such method of doping could also be applied to other wide band gap semiconductors, and that this technique might be more effective than metal doping.  This finding could be crucial for the development of sustainable energy technologies. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Finally, I show that the elastic process remains too elusive to be detected, and the most promising outcome would be an upper limit on the $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ branching ratios of $<0.45\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<1.05\cdot10^{-5}$, which are nonetheless still more stringent than the current limits. This research was motivated by LHCb's forward proton tags in the top-quark pair production analysis, and I discovered that the semi-elastic process is predominantly limited by the expected number of detected proton-proton collisions rather than the ability to identify protons emitted at the front end. By contrast, the fully elastic process appears too inaccessible due to both the expected number of detected proton-proton collisions and the lack of acceptably large solid angles for detecting elastic scattering in the forward direction. Last, I outline the inspiration for, method of analysis, and outcomes of this research in detail. This work was motivated by an analysis of top-quark pair production in the Large Hadron Collider by the LHCb collaboration. I discovered that the most rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ could be identified using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and I demonstrated that the most stringent limits on the branching ratios of these decays would be $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Additionally, we establish a minimum $\lambda$ value for directed versions of the problem, exceeding the former record of $\frac{29}{25}$ for directed triangles and $\frac{19}{15}$ for directed cliques. We also establish a lower bound for the problem of finding a large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ within an infinitely large, randomly edge-filled subgraph of the complete graph, with a density of at least $\lambda$, as being greater than $\frac{7}{5}$ for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and $\frac{4}{3}$ for directed cliques, and provide a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpass the former record of 3/5. We achieve these results by incorporating a generalized version of the "random selection" method developed by Erdos and Galvin, along with a modified "branching" approach. We also use a "directed extension" of our triangle lower bound to demonstrate the efficacy of the "directed approach" for tackling upper density problems within Ramsey theory. We anticipate these generalized methods will serve as precursors for addressing more intricate problems and structures within the field of Ramsey theory. Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. These advantages of qudits stem from reduced functional entropy in qutrits, which facilitates a longer lifetime before information is lost during computation. As a result, qudits offer significant prospects for addressing the fault-tolerance limitations of near-term quantum devices. To achieve this advantage, we propose a qutrit implementation of the Wightman two-point function by defining the qudit Dirac field in an error-tolerant manner, utilizing a basis-agnostic approach that resists interference from unwanted qudit states during production and processing. Our approach to qudits encompasses both continuous-time qutrits and their digital simulations, utilizing a variety of noise-channel models, and incorporating relevant fault-tolerance metrics to demonstrate the efficacy of qutrits over qubits in computation. Our research paves the way for extending qudits to multi-dimensional spacetime and exploring qudits in other complex scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/Stratonidge/qudits-qed. Our results also highlight the importance of distinguishing between coherent and incoherent noise in scalable quantum computations. To achieve this, we propose a simple, efficient digital qudit architecture that can be used as a benchmark for other designs. Our error-tolerance analysis utilizes both average and worst-case entropy metrics, providing a clear and unambiguous indicator of a qudit's durability in the face of noise. Our research demonstrates the practical applications of qudits in addressing the fault-tolerance limitations of near-term quantum devices. To achieve this, we propose a variety of noise-reduction strategies, including qudit-state preparation, digital simulation, and utilization of a variety of noise-channel models. Our code utilizes JAX for high-performance automatic differentiation and Numpy for efficient memory management. Our research initializes the development of a qudits-qed package, which can serve as a foundation for extending this research to other complex scenarios

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. If realized, it could also serve as a hallmark for testing the accuracy of particle simulations used in this work. The degree of polarization might be impacted by the presence of an ion projectile, but remains robust in the case of a thin solid target without it. The most polarization-intensive region, where the positrons are most concentrated, can be analyzed in depth by simulating the experiment using a moving frame of reference, thereby elucidating the underlying physical mechanisms at play. The findings also offer a feasible explanation for the recently observed anomalous electron polarization in the Little Solenoid Experiment conducted at the University of Michigan. The proposed experiment has a reasonable scale and could provide evidence for this predicted effect, thereby offering access to extremely highly polarized positrons with vast applications, including the creation of highly polarized electron and positron beams in particle physics experiments, the study of highly polarized pair production, as well as unique opportunities in condensed matter physics and materials science. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it proves that these groups cannot be simple groups. This work also provides an infinite sequence of finite groups with a polynomial diameter, serving as counterparts to groups with exponentially large diameters, which were previously established by Breuillard and Tointon. This sequence demonstrates that there are infinitely many finite simple groups with a polynomial diameter that are not classified within the existing framework of the classification of finite simple groups. This result also sheds light on the relationship between the diameter of a finite group and its number of conjugacy classes. This research was inspired by a question concerning the existence of finite groups with a polynomial diameter that is larger than any polynomial, and it introduces an analytical framework that can be applied to study the properties of finite groups based on the size of their generating sets. This research builds upon earlier works by Breuillard and Tointon, and Gilraynes, which among other findings, demonstrated that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup, and proved that these groups cannot be simple groups. This research is an extension of the results from Breuillard and Tointon concerning the properties of finite groups with a polynomial diameter, and as such, it should be considered part of the same research project. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor was successfully integrated into a voltage and frequency scaling system, demonstrating a reduction of approximately 20% in energy consumption for workloads executed across the entire temperature range. The design exhibits tremendous scalability, with possibilities of implementation in modern high-density silicon processes like FinFET technologies. The proposed temperature sensor has the potential to be seamlessly embedded into complex systems-on-chip (SoCs). The design's exceptional energy efficiency, combined with its compact size, makes it an ideal solution for use in future temperature-aware and adaptive embedded processors. The development of the temperature sensor was facilitated by extensive use of full-custom design techniques for high-performance, low-power operation. The design has unique applications in advanced CMOS processes, including FinFET technologies, and offers valuable insights into the behavior of sub-threshold MOS devices, with implications for future temperature-aware and adaptive embedded processors. The performance of the temperature sensor was demonstrated across various temperature ranges and supply voltages, highlighting its resilience in real-world scenarios. Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Ultimately, it may pave the way for a revised picture of massive star formation governed by different physical constraints than the one currently understood.  A possible mechanism underlying this observed mass difference is suggested to be dynamic feedback, albeit other explanations such as the influence of molecular cloud turbulence, core interaction, or a varying threshold for protostellar collapse also have plausible grounds. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The validity of our approach is demonstrated through applications to various liquid-gas interfaces, including foams and soap films. The integrated "leverage rule" and roughness factor also enable the prediction of surface stress during stick-slip motion. The discovery of the stationary regime, which has no equivalent in solid mechanics, is particularly noteworthy. The stick-slip regime is known to result in noise and vibrations during the flow of complex liquids, which is a critical issue in power acoustic emission technology that relies on point contact between probe tips and samples. The emergence of the stationary regime in addition to the stick-slip regime could be beneficial for minimizing vibrations and stick-slip noise. The integrated model proposed in this study provides a useful framework for predicting stress during the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces. The discovery of the three distinct friction regimes and the development of a predictive model can be applied to various technical and biological systems that involve fluid-solid interface friction. The development of a predictive model for surface stress during the flow of complex liquids also opens up opportunities for improving power acoustic emission technology by minimizing vibrations and stick-slip noise. The integrated model proposed in this study can be further developed to predict the stress patterns observed during stick-slip motion, which could be beneficial for various technical and biological applications that involve fluid-solid interface friction. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. In addition, an interesting finding shows that look-ahead attention is ineffective when using lattice structures to model target word sequences due to its tendency to prefer target words with shorter neighbor lists. Consequently, this research paper proposes two novel structures, target word buckets and sorted target word lists, that efficiently model target word sequences and integrate look-ahead attention, resulting in a significant boost in translation accuracy. In particular, the NIST Chinese-to-English translation task sees a 13.1% improvement in BLEU scores. All research findings and models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in neural machine translation. Code is available at https://github.com/MILIGHT/look-ahead-attention and models are available at https://github.com/MILIGHT/lattice-free-nmt. All research is built upon the baseline neural machine translation models developed by https://github.com/juhnyang/transformer-translate. The research paper is based on research conducted under the guidance of Ju-Yu Yang at National Taiwan University and Yu Tsao at Academia Sinica. The primary researchers are Ming-Hsiao Hsu, Yu-Hsuan Chen, and Yu-Tsao Hum. Moreover, this research received significant support from Google AI Research Lab, specifically Andrew Maynard-Nones, Yigal Keren, and Orsen Guo, as well as the Ministry of Science and Technology in Taiwan, specifically IIS Technology under Grant Number MOST 109-2639-H-007-001, and the aim is to publish a more comprehensive version in a conference related to natural language processing. The current version will be made available in the conference paper expansion database https://cpb.ipau.li/. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Furthermore, we share the lessons learned to encourage and guide future grid computing developments. Finally, we outline the possibilities offered by a grid computing paradigm that is accessible, yet intuitive, and demonstrate its applicability to various real-world problems and scenarios. By experiencing the benefits of translational research, we encourage others to follow a similar path with their own projects, expressing our own experience as an instance that others can draw from. We hope this experience of ours will be useful to a broad range of researchers and developers. We also view this effort as an opportunity to explore the grid computing paradigm with others, and in doing so, uncover new possibilities and opportunities, as well as contribute to the advancement of this paradigm itself. We are convinced that the grid computing model has vast potential, not just in handling complex computations, but also in providing a straightforward and accessible way to tackle intricate problems that involve multiple disciplines. We demonstrate the versatility of this model by applying it to a problem that appears very different from the ones it was originally designed to solve. We show that a grid-based approach can be successfully used to tackle the problem of inferring the functionality of complex systems from raw data, and present the benefits of doing so in the context of an actual case study. We also outline the technical challenges that arise when employing this method and propose possible solutions, in addition to making the relevant code freely available for the benefit of the scientific community. We hope that our effort will give rise to a new line of research that is focused on applying the grid computing paradigm to address problems of this nature, and make the developed code a useful tool that can be utilized and enhanced by others. We are certain that this approach can be advantageous in other domains, such as those mentioned earlier, and even in fields like biology, finance, and social sciences, and therefore we are making the code generic enough to be applicable in these areas as well. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use effective field theories to describe possible interactions between standard model fields and light sterile neutrinos or sub-GeV dark matter. We analyze J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by incorporating relevant effective operators and considering contributions from both light sterile neutrinos and dark matter. Notably, we find that J/ψ decay into a single photon and a light sterile neutrino could explain the 12σ anomaly reported by the BESIII collaboration, but it cannot account for the 3.3σ anomaly observed by the J-PET experiment. Additionally, J/ψ decay into a single photon and sub-GeV dark matter cannot exceed the LHCb limit by two orders of magnitude. We also explore connections between these effective descriptions and fundamental theories, considering both "leptonic" and "hadronic" Compton processes and calculating cross-sections for the J/ψ production in deep inelastic scattering. Furthermore, we propose an "invisible" J/ψ decay search channel for the J-PET experiment and an "extended" search for the J/ψ → γ + invisible particle process for the BESIII experiment, both of which could verify the existence of light sterile neutrinos or sub-GeV dark matter through J/ψ production. Our predicted rates for these searches are within the capabilities of their existing infrastructure. In the context of light dark matter, we also describe the relevant effective operators for the J/ψ decay into a single photon and light dark matter, but find that such a search is already being conducted by the J-PET experiment. Our predictions for the J/ψ production rates in deep inelastic scattering can be verified by the J-PET and BESIII experiments using their existing J/ψ production infrastructure. Our analysis suggests that J/ψ production in deep inelastic scattering could serve as a benchmark for J/ψ generation models. We provide predicted rates for the J-PET and BESIII experiments, which have the potential to verify the effective descriptions of J/ψ interactions with light sterile neutrinos or sub-GeV dark matter through J/ψ production in deep inelastic scattering. Our research paves the way for further investigation into J/ψ interactions with light sterile neutrinos or sub-GeV dark matter, which could provide a deeper understanding of these effective descriptions. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This involved increasing the size of the plasma chamber's end plugs, and reducing the magnetic field to 0.45 Teslas. As a result, it was possible to produce plasma with an electron density of 10 to the power of 10 per cubic meter, and a relatively long plasma column of 0.7 meters. Consequently, the IShTAR plasma source can now be used for valid plasma interaction research with radio frequency waves in the ICRF regime. Key improvements have been made to the source, and it is currently being used for scientific experiments. A proposal has been made to apply these findings to the design of a new European plasma test facility. A recommendation has been made to include plasma source research in future ICRF facility designs. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Additionally, this approach yields a significant increase in performance when applied to a common point-based annotation method, known as 2D U-Net based annotation, which involves annotating overlapping points on target masks. To further evaluate this approach, it was applied to a publicly available dataset used for automated nucleus detection in cancer diagnosis, which showed improved results when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. To facilitate reproducibility, the code and trained models for this approach were made publicly available. Moreover, it is worthwhile to note that this approach is versatile and can be applied to other medical image segmentation tasks with overlapping objects. We also propose a simple and effective data augmentation technique, which significantly improves the performance of the model when applied to a publicly available nucleus detection dataset in cancer diagnosis. We expect that this approach, along with the proposed data augmentation technique, will contribute to the development of automated nucleus detection algorithms in cancer diagnosis and other medical image segmentation tasks with overlapping objects. We also propose a simple and effective data augmentation technique, which significantly improves the performance of the model when applied to a publicly available nucleus detection dataset in cancer diagnosis. We believe that this approach, along with the proposed data augmentation technique, will facilitate the development of automated nucleus detection algorithms in cancer diagnosis and other medical image segmentation tasks with overlapping objects. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A unified and comprehensive description of GCNNs is thus offered, aiming to enhance the community's understanding and facilitate further research and development of GCNNs. A supporting code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/GCNN_tutorial. A related notebook can be accessed at https://github.com/ghrua/GCNN_notebook. A more extensive notebook with associated data is available at https://github.com/ghrua/GCNN_details. A detailed tutorial on GCNNs, including the underlying mechanics and a step-by-step numerical example, is presented, demonstrating the seamless integration of GCNNs within the broader Neural Network framework. Although GCNNs embody a diverse range of topics, this tutorial approaches them in an accessible and unified manner, replete with supporting code and supplementary materials. A key advantage of GCNNs lies in their capability to effectively process complex and irregular data patterns, despite the intricacy of their structure, which hinders understanding of their internal mechanics. In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then described as non-flat connections, from which conserved charges can be deduced using established formulas, albeit those of standard Chern-Simons theory. The soliton's stability and characteristics are determined based on holonomic constraints along cyclic paths, while in rotating hairy black holes cases, the theory allows recovery of the temperature and chemical potential. The entropy generated by the black holes in these scenarios remains consistent with that predicted by the Chern-Simons theory. The conformal equivalent to this framework describes General Relativity's interaction with a cosmologically constant scalar field. The redefinition of the Chern-Simons form for this system, using suitable composite gauge fields, is explored in a simplified form. The approach here can be extended to include additional scalar fields. The rotating black hole solutions and their associated entropy in these scenarios remain unaffected by the change of variables. The effective action describing this system when expressed in curved variables appears to represent an $R^2$ gravity theory, which in turn can be modified to address the black hole's singularity issue. The de Sitter spacetime's (dS) entropy, both in its disconnected and connected forms, can also be determined using this approach. The dS entropy in the 4-dimensional case turns out to be $\frac{3\pi^2}{2l^2}\Delta l^2$, which differs from the conventional $\frac{\pi^2}{l^2}\Delta l^2$ formula. The 2-dimensional dS entropy, in contrast, adheres to the expected $\frac{2\pi}{\ell}\Delta\ell$ formula. The 4d Anti-de Sitter spacetime's (AdS) entropy, however, remains consistent with the formula $\frac{\pi}{3}N(S)\Delta l^2$, where $N(S)$ is the number of AdS spacetime's supersymmetries. The topological invariant describing the Calabi-Yau's Albanese volume also proves to be accessible through this method.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Ultimately, VSSA elastography exhibits notable advancements in estimating mechanical properties, particularly in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement, and is deemed a promising technique for elastography in deep tissue imaging. Experimental outcomes revealed a 2.45-fold and 4.33-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of lateral displacement estimation in the muscle and liver tissues respectively when using VSSA in comparison to SA, and a 2.45-fold increase in the estimation of Young's modulus in the liver tissue. Nonetheless, the VSSA technique faces notable constraints related to its increased side lobe levels and spatio-temporal variations in sampling frequencies; these limitations necessitate further research into techniques that mitigate these drawbacks. This study proposes a novel variance-based quality factor (QF) estimator for evaluating the image quality in elastography, defined as the variance of the elastic modulus estimate, demonstrating a 1.68-fold increase in the variance-based QF in VSSA elastography in comparison to SA. This study proposes the use of re-weighted least squares (RWS) for addressing the speckle noise variability in sampling frequencies, demonstrating a 2.45-fold increase in the SNR of lateral displacement estimation in the muscle tissue when employing RWS in comparison to the standard least squares method.
