Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This innovation enables the automatic generation of pseudocodes from high-level descriptions, providing a practical application for the principles of logical pseudocodes. As a tangible demonstration of this methodology, we present a doxology regarding the fundamental theorem of symmetric functions, presented in a manner that can be translated to pseudocodes automatically. This example pseudocode can be generated from a high-level description utilizing logical pseudocodes, and it showcases the capabilities of this framework in a notable mathematical context. Moreover, this doxology proves the fundamental theorem, which is a notable achievement in itself. In addition to this example, we also offer a set of basic protocols for efficient data processing, leveraging the capacity for forward reasoning. These protocols are essentially a set of pseudocodes that can be generated automatically from a high-level description, and they embody a fundamental equivalence between imperative algorithms and logical proofs with cut operations, offering a meaningful contribution to the ongoing discussion on the relationship between them. Furthermore, this doxology has practical implications, as it can be utilized to develop reliable and efficient programs for calculating symmetric functions, demonstrating the practical value of this framework. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by conducting simulations involving mock data. Furthermore, we outline the prerequisites and our algorithm's construction in greater detail. Ultimately, our contribution addresses a notable gap in the dynamics stream setting for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. We also leverage our core algorithm to enhance the coherence of a prominent stream clustering problem variant, known as the sliding window $k$-means problem. Our algorithm's performance is assessed through comprehensive numerical experiments. We additionally provide a straightforward method to extend our core algorithm for addressing the sliding window $k$-means problem, thereby obtaining a more precise analysis of the optimal algorithm space complexity for this particular problem variant. Ultimately, our research reveals an intriguing contrast between the optimal algorithm space complexity for the sliding window $k$-means problem and its dynamic fragment, and the optimal algorithm space complexity for the sliding window dynamic fragment and its parent problem, the $k$-means clustering problem. Both instances demonstrate an optimal algorithm space complexity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, along with linear dependence on $k$ and $d$ dimensions. We also explore the relationship between coreset algorithms and sliding window fragments of common clustering problems, drawing a broad generalization from our specific findings. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Our approach ensures that the Prince agent always pursues the King agent along the shortest path possible. Our approach has been published in the 2023 Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Robotics. Note: This abstract is a condensed version of a full paper that is currently under review. Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness and efficiency of our
simple yet efficient sub-network isolation approach, providing insights into
the dynamics of shared representations in multi-task settings. Our code is available
at https://github.com/kuangshu/single-dynamics-multiple-tasks. Our study
contributes to the understanding of shared dynamics in multi-task settings and
provides an accessible framework for exploring the benefits and limitations of
learning single dynamics models for multiple tasks. Our approach can be viewed

isolation during policy execution, which we plan to explore in future work. Our
results demonstrate the potential of using sub-network isolation in multi-task
reinforcement learning, even without task-specific policy learning, and shed
light on the dynamics of shared representations in dynamics models. Our approach
has an added benefit of making the learned dynamics more robust against over-
parameterization, which we observe through our experiment and further
investigation. Our code is available at https://github.com/kuangshu/single-dynamics-multiple-tasks. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our method includes a mechanism for regularizing the target sample, a Wasserstein generator initializer, and a technique for boosting convergence through regularized sample generation. Our proposals are straightforward to incorporate into existing GAN training routines. We also presented our framework's versatility by incorporating external knowledge, prior images that guide the sampling process, which significantly enhanced the GAN's performance in certain tasks. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Consequently, we emphasize the significance of examining fractional-order models with linear invariant subspaces in particular cases. Finally, we outline possible future research directions and opportunities presented by the study of fractional-order dynamical systems. Invariant sets have been a long-standing subject of study in mathematics, particularly in the context of planar systems. However, their intersection with stability theory has been given relatively little attention, and this is particularly true for fractional-order systems. Thus, this article aims to provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on this topic. In addition to the theoretical foundations, we will also review the available numerical methods for detecting invariant sets, with a specific focus on the use of fill-in plots. Furthermore, we will discuss some illustrative numerical examples demonstrating the application of these methods in different dynamical systems, including a famous pendulum model and a mass-following model. Ultimately, this article will conclude by highlighting the prospects and challenges presented by the study of fractional-order dynamical systems and invariant sets within the stability framework. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Another screen, named Screen D, was also discovered in the same line of sight to PSR B1133+16 in the Sco-Cen star-forming region, which may be linked to a molecular cloud at a distance of 7.5 parsecs. Screen D's velocity suggests it could be moving towards the Sun, and it's likely that this screen could be responsible for the limited observing time available for this particular pulsar. Overall, this study demonstrates long-term observations are necessary to uncover the complex screens in the interstellar medium and their ever-changing scintillation patterns. Additionally, it highlights the capability of high-resolution scintillation observations to reveal details about screen velocities, orientations, and distances. Lastly, it is evident that the Local Bubble is not a uniform screen over large scales, and there are likely many isolated voids similar to the one found in this research. The methods used here can be applied to study screens in the lines of sight to other pulsars, providing a unique window into the structure and dynamics of the interstellar medium. The research suggests that the medium surrounding the Earth is more complex than previously believed, with varying void and screen sizes that could impact the detection and duration of observations for specific pulsars. The velocity of screens can affect the scintillation patterns, possibly contributing to the limited observing time for some pulsars, and their orientations affect the visibility of voids, offering insights into the geometry of the interstellar medium that can be applied to areas beyond the Local Bubble. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, QPNet is applied to generate waveforms for speech texts outside the training frequency range, yielding superior results when compared to baseline methods. The proposed model provides a versatile framework for quasi-periodic waveform generation and has substantial potential applications in speech and other signal processing tasks. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this approach leads to an easy demonstration of the injectivity of the shadow construction, as well as its varietal properties. Lastly, this framework enables the straightforward extension of Morita invariance to shadow constructions across various subcategories of bicategories. A notable corollary arises from this invariance, demonstrating the injectivity of the structure of a bicategorical extensivity monad, as well as the morphism monad for distributive laws, both of which were previously unknown. A preceding understanding of basic notions from category theory, topology, and algebra is required to fully comprehend this research.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. We develop a video sound source localization model using only positively labeled samples. To achieve this, a new approach is taken where a synthetic overcomplete set of sound sources is initially modeled and then a GAN-based network is used to explore the video domain and mine difficult samples, which are defined as areas with sound emissions but unclear visuals. These difficult samples serve as the positive training set for the model's sound source localization network. Our method succeeds in localization sound sources even when the visual information is incomplete or misleading due to several distortions being applied to the training data, including large orientation changes, mask garbled, and distorted faces. Our approach demonstrates substantial improvements in accuracy compared to baseline methods using manually labeled data, as well as other unsupervised methods, on the Flickr SoundNet dataset. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/lewisui/UnsupSourcLoc.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN achieves comparable performance to Euclidean-based GCNs on distantly embedded graphs. This confirms the importance of geometric adherence in graph representation and highlights LGCN's effectiveness across various graph embeddings. This paper is an extended version of a previous paper that was presented at IJCAI 2023. Experimental evaluations have been expanded to include six additional datasets, and the paper now includes an in-depth analysis of hyperbolic graph learning's robustness to Euclidean-based GCNs. This version also includes an updated Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) with improved performance. This version has a distinct neural network architecture based on the Lorentzian version of the graph convolutional network, and it has the advantage of being trainable using standard backpropagation methods. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Ultimately, this is achieved through a compactness-uniqueness argument, where we show that a sequence of distinct solutions, obtained by using an infinite number of measurements, cannot exist. An additional contribution explores the case where the source term and part of the initial conditions lie within certain smooth functions space. In this scenario, uniqueness is demonstrated through an additional regularity condition. An illustrative numerical example utilizing a beam and an airbox structure as the acoustic wave equation system is presented. Furthermore, we propose an iterative Bilinear Regression algorithm to solve the inverse problem. This involves using the Euler implicit scheme for discretization. A priori and bilinear regression-based error estimates are derived, along with the solution and its regularity. A key aspect of this research involves addressing the issue of growing solution when using the Euler implicit scheme for the plate equation. This is achieved by leveraging the compactness-uniqueness argument and obtaining the necessary regularity for the initial conditions. A priori and a posteriori error estimates are established in various $L^2$ norm spaces. A numerical example demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed algorithm. Ultimately, this inverse problem finding has implications for source signal identification in complex structural acoustic systems. This research contributes to a better understanding of uniqueness, stability, and numerical solution approaches for source term identification within these systems. A key aspect of this research involves developing a novel Bilinear Regression algorithm for this problem, which has not been previously addressed. This algorithm is tested alongside a Bilinear Regression algorithm using the Euler implicit scheme for a beam and an airbox structure as the acoustic wave equation system. A numerical example utilizing this algorithm for a realistic helicopter structure (airbox) and a wing structure as the acoustic wave equation system is also provided. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  However, this particular gauge does not result in a gauge-invariant effective action.  An analysis of the underlying differential operator reveals that it corresponds to the harmonic Riemann operator when the background is flat, and this allows discussing the choice of gauge in relation to other harmonic gauge choices, including the de Donder gauge, which serves as a reference point.  The paper also examines the impact of the harmonic gauge choice when imposing linearized spontaneous symmetry breaking and determines the suitable gauge choice.  A previous misunderstanding regarding the value of the massive vector field Compton wavelength also arises in this context, and the correct calculation shows that the Compton wavelength doesn't depend on the gauge choice.  An examination of the paper's results through the lens of the harmonic gauge theory provides Compton wavelength values of 1.84 times the Planck length and the 1.92 times the Planck length cited in the original paper, respectively. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. Furthermore, the canonical representation is linked to the classical dynamics of its underlying Hamiltonian, demonstrating how its associated dynamics are interlinked with the matrix that defines the thermal state. Ultimately, the success of this approach is demonstrated through the validation of multiple established thermal equilibrium state properties, including the partition function, correlation functions, and the energy density, using the metaplectic operator framework. Lastly, the generality of this framework is highlighted by applying it to a random Hamiltonian dynamics. The resulting expression obtained through this method is found to be interchangeable with other established techniques in the literature. The utility of this approach is also shown to extend beyond the thermal equilibrium state, by successfully generating both the quantum and classical time-dependent states for any given Hamiltonian dynamics. The underlying metaplectic operator for a random Hamiltonian dynamics is found to be statistically equivalent to its random matrix counterpart. The overall goal of this work is to make the concept of negative absolute temperature more accessible to undergraduate students by connecting it to familiar two-level systems. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, in Ru based oxides, $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can affect the relative weights of different spin-orbital interactions by up to two orders of magnitude, influencing the strong coupling spin-orbital nematic phase behavior. Nonetheless, despite $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing being inevitable in these materials, it is noteworthy that many experimental branching ratios are often explained without considering this effect, which we argue may complicate the understanding of transition metal oxides' complex physics. Nonetheless, incorporating $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can also offer additional adjustable parameters, facilitating fitting of experimental data. To facilitate practical application, we provide an explicit example analysis of Ba$_2$RuO$_5$ clustering about the Ru site, demonstrating that the relevant parameters can be evaluated through crystallographic Ru-O bond lengths. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of considering $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing in the theoretical modeling of transition metal oxides' magnetic properties and phases. To facilitate widespread use, the necessary codes for this study are available at this link https://github.com/spinorbitseparation/cubic_d_orbitals. We also outline possible extensions to other geometric configurations and filling patterns in the appendix. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Lastly, it provides an appendix with supplementary information on the related mathematical concepts of I-functions, FJRW, and birational transformations.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is particularly suited
for researchers, scientists, and educators in fields like geography, biology,
medicine, and social sciences. The package includes sample data sets and
tutorials to help users master the tool. Version 1.0 of ViDaExpert runs on Windows. Version 0.96 is also available for Linux and Mac OS X, but without 3D viewing capabilities. Version 0.96 includes an Excel add-in for data import. Both versions include sample data sets and tutorials. ViDaExpert was created by Giuseppe Caruso and is offered as a free download. It is used in various academic courses and research projects. One such project involves analyzing soil spectral data with PCA and elastic maps. Another project utilizes ViDaExpert for teaching spatial analysis in biology. It has also been utilized in environmental and kinetic studies. One study employed ViDaExpert with K-Means clustering for analyzing 16s RNA gene data. Another application of ViDaExpert involves using linear discriminant analysis for diagnosing plant diseases. Another research project leverages ViDaExpert for teaching machine learning in ecology. One study used ViDaExpert with decision tree construction for analyzing remote sensing data. Another project of research used ViDaExpert with multilinear regression for analyzing nutritional data from mass spectrometry. Another application of ViDaExpert involves using PCA and elastic maps for analyzing protein structures. One research project utilized ViDaExpert with K-Means clustering for analyzing genomic data. Another course that utilizes ViDaExpert is a graduate course in geography that uses ViDaExpert for teaching spatial analysis. ViDaExpert has the capability to analyze spatial data with weights in weighted PCA. It is possible to perform elastic maps in ViDaExpert using different distance metrics. It is possible to construct decision tree models in ViDaExpert with different criteria. It is possible to construct linear discriminant analysis models in ViDaExpert with or without weights.
